PRIVILEGE-MR. FERLAND DISMISSAL OF CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAY EMPLOYEES AT JOLIETTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question
of privilege. When the House met yesterday, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), who seems to be more affected than any one else by the stifling heat which we are experiencing these days, forgot himself to the extent of using language, in referring to me, which I can only describe as improper. The hon. Minister of Railways asserted that at a public meeting held in Joliette, on July 1, last, I had made misstatements. He based his assertions on a report published in "L'Etoile du Nord" of Joliette, a well-meaning newspaper, whose report, however, is not complete and accurate on certain points. May I, Sir, correct the statement made by the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion). At that meeting held on July 1, I first expressed my disappointment to the people of Joliette as regards the decision taken by the management of the Canadian National Railways in dismissing 46 employees working in the railway shops at Joliette, 40 of whom were employed in the car-repair department, the other 6 belonged to the locomotive shop. I stated that this decision was arbitrary, unjust and illegal. It is unjust because, in this same section of the central division, when the Canadian National Railway's management found it necessary to reduce their staff in other localities they did so in a ratio of 10 to 20 per cent, while in Joliette, a reduction of two thirds was effected in the car-repair shops. I also stated that this decision was illegal, because it was carried out in violation of an existing contract between the Canadian National Railway and the city of Jolieitte, definitely binding the former, a contract which Sir Henry Thornton, President of the Canadian National Railway deemed it his duty to acknowledge and fulfil when previously a delegation made up of the members of the Chamber of Commerce and the city council of Joliette discussed the matter with him. Finally, I stated that on a question of vital importance and national interest to the town of Joliette, I thought that it behooved the hon. Minister of Railways to intervene when a request was made ito him in order to

Privilege-Mr. Ferland
prevent an injustice being perpetrated or a contract violated. I then publicly stated, that when I heard of the decision taken by the Canadian National Railways, I immediately communicated with the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals who to my great amazement, answered by letter that this matter came entirely under the Canadian National Railways management and that I should acknowledge with him that it would be useless for a delegation from Joliette to come to Ottawa.
In order to well establish the facts concerning the blame which I attach to the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion)-not with reference to his receiving a delegation, nor to having closed the door on a delegation which had arrived in Ottawa, but as regards his attitude on that occasion-I shall read the letter which I sent to the hon. Minister and his answer. I contend that this answer is evidence of his refusal to arbitrate in the matter and to listen to our grievances, and, even more, it is a declaration to the effect that it would serve no purpose for a delegation to come to Ottawa.
My letter is dated June 26, last and reads as follows:
(Text)
Dear Mr. Manion:
You will please find enclosed a telegram which I received this morning from Mr. Hector Mainville of Joliette, regarding the Canadian National Railway's decision to lay off forty men out of sixty men now employed in car department at Joliette, Quebec.
May I venture to say that the above decision is in violation of the terms of an existing contract which obliges the Canadian National Railways to maintain in permanence at Joliette (one of its divisional points) not less than fifty men in that car department, according to the interpretation of Canadian National Railways officials?
I wish you would kindly investigate and see that no unlawful act or injustice is done.
With my best regards, I remain, sir,
Yours truly,
Charles E. Ferland.
The telegram which I enclosed, and which was addressed to myself in Ottawa, reads as follows:
Officially decided by Canadian National officials that effective July first forty men out of sixty will be laid off in car department whereas at other points in this district reduction only amounts from ten to twenty per cent. Conditions most disastrous and delegation wants to meet you at your office soon as possible.
Again, on the 29th of June, I received a letter from the Minister of Railways and Canals reading as follows:
Dear Mr. Ferland,

I have received your communication of the 26th instant, and will pass it on to the railway 22110-227
management for their consideration, as the matter is one entirely in the hands of the officials. You will, therefore, appreciate that the deputation should see the management and that there would really be no use in their coming to Ottawa.

I rise to a question of privilege and say to the house that the last statement in the speech of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is incorrect.
(Translation): The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, made, in the last part of his speech, a statement which calls for a denial. He said:
I have brought this matter up, Mr. Speaker, because the hon. gentleman has been in the habit-this is not the first time-of making such mis-statements.
I wish to say to the hon. Minister of Railways that it ill becomes him to make off-hand charges which he cannot substantiate. I have made certain speeches in the House, in the course of my short stay in Ottawa, and I have held joint meetings during the last election, in five or six counties, however, never was any body able to point out that I had made mis-statements. In concluding my remarks and in order to be clearly understood, I shall use towards my hon. friend the same language

he used in making his charge against me: "I think there is decency and honesty in public life that should be respected even by the hon. Minister of Railways."

Neither the hon. member nor anyone else asked me to see a deputation, and for that reason I could not refuse.
In regard to the question of privilege which the hon. member now raises concerning my remarks about his statements at other times, I make the statement that in the past few years in the province of Quebec the hon. gentleman was one of the worst offenders in regard to the supposed Turkish and Egyptian wars.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
when this bill was introduced and when the Prime Minister made his speech to the house on its second reading, lion, members and the public generally assumed that the tariff board which was being created was one which would hear the representations of parties who might be interested in any tariff changes proposed, or with respect to changes in the tariff which already had been made. I have no doubt they believed that once the tariff board was appointed the parties of their own volition or at least at the instance of the board itself might appear before the board to make representations with respect to proposed or actual changes in the tariff as they might affect different parties, either manufacturers, consumers, labour, those connected with the primary industries or any other class or any individual in the community.
The discussion on the measure however has made perfectly clear that such in fact is not the intention in connection with the proposed tariff board. The powers of the tariff board will of course be exercised in accordance with the provisions of the statute. Whether it will have the right tio exercise those powers at all, however, will depend on the terms of the instructions given by the Minister of Finance. Such restrictions mean that so far as the board is concerned, as regards its relation to the public, its usefulness is entirely restricted to such purposes as the Minister of Finance may himself direct. Such conditions are, I believe, wholly at variance with what the public conceives to be the real advantage of a tariff board.
I notice that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) is about to leave the chamber, and if it is convenient I would ask him to remain a moment or two so that I may address a special word to him. As hon. members are aware the Minister of Justice has always had great facility for presenting an argument clearly and forcibly. In 1912 w'hen a previous government brought down a bill for the creation of a tariff commission my hon. friend was sitting with the Liberal opposition, 22110-2271
and at that time he presented the Liberal point of view with respect to the measures then before the house. The objections which the present Minister of Justice then urged in connection with that bill are in the main the objections which we are now making to the bill which has been introduced by the government of which he is now a member.
I shall read to hon. members a part of the speech delivered by my hon. friend on February 13, 1912, in connection with the bill respecting a tariff commission which was before the house on that date. I shbll refer only to those parts of his speech which bear directly on similar features which appear in the present proposed legislation. In listening to his criticism the house may assume that I am stating the contentions of the Liberal opposition of to-day with respect to the measure now before us. The present Minister of Justice on that occasion spoke as follows. The quotation will be found at page 2940 and subsequent pages of Hansard, Yol. 2, Session 1911-12:
The board has no power to initiate anything, no power to take a single step without the special instructions of the Minister of Finance or the governor in council. I understood, when the bill was first brought in that the board was an independent and permanent board of inquiry, and would be instituted to make, apart from any special instructions from anybody, the inquiries set out in subsection 1 of section 4. But when wre come down to analyze the sections of the bill, we find that the functions of the board are subject to the direction of the minister. They cannot enter upon an inquiry, they cannot make a suggestion. they cannot do any of the things which the bill contemplates they should do, and which the public believe they are to do and which are made the main excuse for the introduction of the bill.
A little further on he said:
Is it not so that the whole design and scope of the bill is to furnish the finance minister and his party with special information, in disregard of the rights of the house and of the people in general to receive that information? To my mind, the bill would be far less objectionable if these words were eliminated as I have sugested.
Then he proceeded:
Here is a board of commissioners, a permanent and so-called independent board of commissioners who cannot make a move in gaining the information or facts which the government deems it important to know, which cannot even start an investigation without the positive direction of the minister. And when that investigation is completed, the report must be made to the minister. The matter starts with the minister, and, so far as this clause goes, it ends with the minister.
He continued:
But where do the members of this house come in; where do the people of the country

come in? I am very strongly of the opinion that if this commission is to report, it should report to parliament and not to the minister. It may be beyond the power of members of this house either to get the result of the inquiry or the evidence on which the results are based if the bill is allowed to go in its present form. -but we do object to these facts being elicited by any secret process and only by special directions.

He was speaking of the way statistics are gathered in Great Britain.
They are collated and published under the authority of the board of trade, the president of which is a member of the cabinet. Why not adopt the British system in preference to this cheap Yankee device?
That was the contemptuous reference made at that time by my hon. friend to similar legislation inspired from the same source. Then a little further on he continued:
What is now proposed is a system modelled in fact upon the United States system. You appoint a permanent board the members of which are not clerks in any sense of the word. They are commissioners with high standing; you have exalted and dignified them, and you are preparing to pay them handsome salaries; you are giving them very wide and high powers; but these men, an independent board appointed for the purpose of acquiring information, cannot move hand or foot until the Minister of Finance beckons to them what to do; and upon getting the word from him as to how they shall proceed, there is no doubt that they will proceed in accordance with his wishes and those of the government of the day.
Finally my hon. friend says:
I want to point out this contingency: Suppose there is a demand on the part of the public to have a certain industry investigated, for instance, the shoe manufacturing industry, and the finance minister does not think it shoidd be investigated. Should not the tariff commission of their own motion, be entitled to go into that question?
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary for me to add a word after quoting what the present Minister of Justice said at the time he was expressing his honest convictions of a measure identical in the features to which I have referred with the bill which is now before the house. May I point out that when this bill was being drafted and con-

sidered in the cabinet the Prime Minister had sitting at his right hand the present Minister of Justice-the one who had pointed out these limitations, these shortcomings, these restrictions, these faults and these frauds, in a similar measure when brought before this house a good many years ago. subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT, POWERS, DUTIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this very matter I could refer to a speech still older than the one quoted by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). But I agree with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie); in fact I think if every hon. member of this house examined his conscience he would find that in the course of twenty-five years he has changed his mind in connection with many things. Whether or not he stayed with one party is immaterial, because party allegiance and sincere expressions of opinion are two entirely different things.
I simply wish to point out what seems to me an important aspect of this piece of legislation which has received little attention. It is partly dealt with by the amendment proposed by the right hon. leader of the opposition, and for that reason I will support that amendment, but I do not think it goes far enough. During the course of this debate I have been struck with the repeated assertion of the Prime Minister that the object of this measure is to create a court of law. No one is more qualified than the Prime Minister to define what is a court of law, and of course from a purely legal standpoint it would be ridiculous and impertinent
on my part to enter into a discussion with him. But I have given some time during my life to the study of constitutional developments, and if there has been one marked feature in the development of British institutions, representative or judicial, it is the tendency to separate judicial powers from legislative or executive powers. This has been done constantly, and for what purpose? It has been done to enable the citizens, the common people of the country, to have recourse to some body of supposedly impartial men to obtain justice, whether in matters of criminal law, civil law or administrative law. I think it may be stated that the basic principle of the judicial system in British communities to-day is that all courts of law should be available to all citizens of the country in order that justice may be done, provided that the matter referred to the court is within the jurisdiction of that court. Certain matters of law are within the jurisdiction of the superior court, while others come under district or circuit courts. There are other courts of still more limited jurisdiction. Certain types of cases come before the exchequer court, and we also have the various courts of appeal. But I think this is the first instance in the whole history of Canada of the creation of a court to which no citizen of Canada will be able to appeal. This is a court of law put up bj' the government for its own convenience, to which the only party who can apply is the Minister of Finance. The leader of the opposition suggests that whenever the government plans a change in the tariff this so-called court of law should be open to people who may be interested in opposing that change.

that time but at any time; it should be open to anyone who has a grievance with respect to the tariff.

speechtext:
The amendment reads:
By making provision that any person feeling himself aggrieved by any existing or proposed tariff provision shall have the right to present his case before the tariff board.
I did not hear the word "existing;" now I am enabled to support the amendment with all my heart. If this is adopted it will broaden the jurisdiction of this board to coincide precisely with what, in my young
Tariff Board

audacity, I proposed to the parliament of Canada at least twenty-five if not thirty years ago, when I found, to my amazement and disappointment, that, in spite of all professions of faith while in opposition, it was not true that there was a protectionist party and a free trade party, because the free trade party advocated free trade while in opposition but maintained protection while in power. At that time I made the suggestion to the old parliament that since protection was the accepted policy, and probably would remain so for many years to come, we should make at least some attempt to introduce into the management and application of our tariff some degree of efficiency, of scientific findings and of stability, with a sufficient degree of elasticity to permit such changes as might be necessary from year to year or from parliament to parliament to meet the exigencies of the situation. I then pointed out what for many years had been the policy pursued in France. In matters purely political I am not an admirer of the French system, but in matters economic I think there is no modern countiy that has been ruled more sensibly than the French nation, perhaps because they have been so foolishly ruled in other matters.
In France the situation was this: The politicians, feeling the uncertainty of the situation, with the very frequent changes of government, realized that at least the economic stability of the country should not be disturbed by changes in the composition of the parliament and of the cabinet. The result has been that although they have adopted the principle of protection and have followed it for many years past, they have not gone to extremes. In fact I think it might be said that apart from the short period of about one-half the reign of Napoleon II'I, after a treaty had been negotiated by Cobden between France and England, France has been the most consistently protective country in Europe. It did not go to the extremes to which Germany went or the extremes to which the United States has gone, or to which we are going now; but they have maintained the principle of protection. In the application of iheir tariff, however, they have introduced some practices which I think could be fruitfully studied by us and applied to a certain extent.
I have already pointed out the inconvenience of having only two models before us, England and the United States. Conditions in England are so different from conditions here that we cannot copy the economic policy of that country; that goes without saying. For many reasons which I am not

going to expound now, I think it equally dangerous to copy as servilely as we have been doing for the last thirty or forty years the policy of the United States. If we do that with the idea that we will reap the same results they have reaped, then we are living and playing in a fool's paradise. We need not imagine that by following servilely the extreme protectionist policy of the United States-and reaping the same evil consequences-we are going to make of Canada a self-sustaining country. If we cherish that idea, then, I repeat, we are living in a fool's paradise: For we shall never make of Canada a cotton-growing country. We shall never make of Canada a coaliproducing country, to the same degree as the United States, and supplying all the varieties of coal which are needed in a northern country like Canada. We can never make Canada a country geographically situated and composed like the United States with that enormous Mississippi valley crossing from north to south, which creates a current of trade in all directions. We cannot expect the same geographical conditions in Canada. We shall never be able to create and maintain an internal trade such as exists in the United States, where there is a population of 110,000,000 of consumers. We cannot hope to have such a trade in this country so long as our population remains as small as it is-and it will be comparatively small for many years to come-and scattered over an area larger than that of the country to the south of us.
We need foreign trade and therefore a tariff board like this should consider every question bearing upon trade. It should consider not only the conditions of production of industries; it should consider not only those various matters that are enumerated in the bill, but it should consider also what commercial results are likely to follow from the operations of the tariff on each industry. The board should consider whether by protecting this or that industry we are not hampering this or that trade, or the relations of Canada with this or that country that can produce similar goods at a cheaper cost than we can produce them in Canada-countries with a larger consuming community, enabling their industries to dispose of their surplus products under better and more advantageous conditions. In other words, you cannot view the simple question of industrial production without taking into consideration not only those factors which govern the production of the same articles in other countries, but the whole problem of trade internal and external.

Tariff Board
Taking the economic situation as it is, considering the needs and the exigencies of all classes of our population, I say that a board of this nature should be open to all claimants in all the provinces of Canada. The gardeners of Canada should be in a position to come and petition the board. The consumers of the west and the producers of the east, so far as manufactured goods are concerned, or, vice versa, the consumers of the east and the producers of the west, with respect to farm products, should be perfectly free to appeal to this so-called court of law for a hearing, in order that justice might be done. Every class in the community should be free to appear before this body constituted by the government to find out all the facts bearing upon our economic situation. All classes of our population should be as free to appeal to this court of law as the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue.
It is too late in the history of our institutions for us to countenance the idea that a parliament, which claims to be a democratic body representing the people, which claims to reflect the views of all the people, representing the interests and the exigencies of the country at large, should disguise as a closed court of law of this kind, what as a matter of fact is and ought to remain an administrative body, but an administrative body subject, if you like, to the authority of the government. I have no objection to its being subject to the government, because the government is responsible to parliament and parliament to the people. And when the people find out that they have made a mistake in giving a majority to this party or the other they may change the administration. But pending such changes, I submit that it is contrary to the basic principles of our parliamentary and judicial institutions to create a body which will be under the sole and exclusive jurisdiction of the minister, a body which will act or remain idle according to the caprice of that minister, shutting its doors to all the interests of Canada. It is from that point of view and solely from that point of view that I object to the bill now before us.
If it was not for the reason I have given, I would entirely support the bill; because, as I have said, over twenty-five years ago I proposed the creation of a tariff board. I suggested it to my good friend, Sir Wilfrid Laurier; and he came very near adopting it, about the same time that he created the railway commission. I said to him:	Since
you are bound to maintain a tariff, why do you not establish a permanent board which
will investigate all tariff questions whenever called upon to do so-a board which will receive requests and counter-requests, proposals and counter-proposals; a board which will give a hearing to all classes and individuals who are interested in the tariff, whether it be to have it raised or lowered. Such a board would reduce to a certain extent the volume of your daily labours and would furnish you with all the elements, if necessary, of a yearly revision of the tariff. You would have figures, statistics and findings, internal and external, from year to year upon which parliament could rely. It could be a court of equity, but above all it should be a court of record, to which all those who wished to appear, to submit their views, would have access. That is what I suggested to Sir Wilfrid Laurier. And if the present government had proposed a measure of that nature I would have supported it.

I can understand why
my hon. friends cannot appreciate my point of view, but I forgive them. For a short while I was myself a party man and I could not believe that a man could have a free mind. However, I freed myself and since that time I have determined to be independent. Of course, I have to make a choice. One cannot clasp one's hands all the time and pray for some extraordinary light to fall from heaven; one must decide on what is at hand. Until now I have not opened my mouth during the whole of this debate, because, being in favour of proper legislation along this line, I have been hoping that something would develop that would enable me to support the bill. But I find the Prime Minister bent upon making of this body a court of law empowered to do a great deal that a court of law can do, although its constitution is repugnant to the very principle of any court of law. Three men are here given the power to infringe upon individual or even political and civil liberty, putting men into jail if need be, as pointed out by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). This so-called court of law is given all these powers; yet at the same time it is to be prevented from acting as a court of law, giving every man a fair hearing. If it were made simply an administrative body, a body constituted for the purpose of giving information to the government, with no powers which it might exercise over any class of our citizens, then, though I might describe it as rather impotent, it would not be obnoxious. But it is being given powers that are repugnant to all the
Tariff Board

interests of the people, and is given no powers which will make it useful to all classes and individuals in the country. For this reason I shall support the amendment and vote against the third reading of the bill.

for changing, on the part of the right hon. gentleman opposite (Mr. Mackenzie King), will end. The Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation was created under the terms of P.C. 530 of April 7, 1926, for the purpose of advising the Minister of Finance in regard to tariff, taxation and other related matters.

Certainly not, but it
was what was set up as a tariff board in lieu of a court, and the reason why the initiative rested with the Minister of Finance is the reason which the house has heard ad nauseam during the last few days, namely, the supremacy of parliament. Why is it that these applications must originate from the Minister of Finance? Because the ultimate responsibility for all tariff action rests with the government of the day, and it is through that minister that the government takes the responsibility so that parliament may act upon the initiative of the government.
[Mr. Bourassa.l
That is the reason. We have heard, during the last four or five days, the right hon. gentleman declaiming to high heaven that parliament is having its power crushed, we have heard that echoed and reechoed, until we are sick of the echo-that this was so, and that that was so-and now we find him rising in his place and declaiming against that very principle and declaring that anybody may go to the tariff board and make application without reference to government or parliamentary control in any way, shape or form. That is what hon. members are driven to for purely political reasons. The tariff board was good enough in 1926, but no application could be made to it except through the Minister of Finance. That was the case in 1927, 1928 and 1929. I heard the right hon. gentleman in those days pointing out the soundness of the measure and what it meant to the consumers of the country, but yet no application could be made except through the Minister of Finance. The reason is so obvious, so clear, so plain; you are not going to create any organization to report upon tariffs that has no relation to the government of the day and the parliament of which that government is the committee. The committee of this house that is reponsible for government to-day is called the cabinet. It is a committee of the House of Commons, and the responsibility of that cabinet is that it goes out of office unless at all times it can command the support of a majority of the members of the house. That being so, it is provided that there must be somewhere some responsible minister for every action that is taken with respect to the government of this country.
The action taken in this case is that of the minister when he sets in motion, by making a request of the board, the machinery whereby the information is obtained. How can this be otherwise? Are you going to have this board cluttered up by having everybody send in applications for changes in the tariff, or to have a minister responsible to parliament to deal with those applications? Is it to be order or disorder, method or lack of it? Is it to be responsibility of parliament or not? Hon. gentlemen opposite say: Give us disorder; give us no method; give us lack of control; give us anything that will enable us to talk, to address the language of the demagogue to the populace about a government that denies them the use of a court. The right hon. gentleman has been declaiming to high heaven about the rights of the people being taken away from them and their

having no opportunities to air their grievances. Everyone knows no government can remain in power that long defies public opinion.

H he fails to make the reference, he subjects himself to a vote of censure of parliament. That is parliamentary government. One method is chaos and disorder; the other is orderly government of the country's affairs. The latter :s consistent and consonant with that principle upon which our institutions have grown up, of parliamentary responsibility and of every minister being responsible to parliament for the exercise, while in office, of his discretion.
In this case an amendment has been set lose which will violate every principle of parliamentary government, disregard every rule that has heretofore prevailed with respect to ministerial responsibilities, and say that everybody on the street may make an application which the board is bound to hear. That is mot my conception of the idea the Canadian people have with respect to matters of this kind. The right hon. gentleman did not have to go back nineteen or twenty years to find, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) says, opinions which they are perfectly welcome to take now that he has discarded them. Tariff Board
been arguing that this board is not a board which makes any tariffs; that it is only a fact-finding board; that its powers are quite innocuous and only for the purpose of making researches with respect to cost productions and things of that kind. Now he has suddenly decided that it is part of the instrument of government and vitally concerns the principle of the responsibility of parliament. I asked my right hon. friend yesterday if he would give an undertaking that before any change, any decrease or increase of duty were made, the case would be referred to the tariff board. His answer was in his usual dogmatic form: He will not. That means that it is going to depend altogether on the minister what applications shall go before the board, and that the minister does not propose to act in the way in which the previous advisory board was administered and permit people to go before that board when they desire to do so. That is the difference between the administration of the board to which he has referred and the administration of this new board.
May I say one thing more? My hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has made the point clearly and distinctly that this house is now being invited to sanction the formation and organization, not of some tariff advisory board, not of any committee, not of any research council, but of something that is going to have the solemnity of a court of record, of something to which, to use the words of the Minister of Justice, men are to be appointed with handsome salaries, eminent men, he said, men of great dignity. That is the way he described them in 1912. He went on to say: After you have got all this splendid organization, what is going to happen? It is not going to start at all. Those were the words of the Minister of Justice in 1912, and I say that unless this amendment passes, that is exactly what will happen in this case. We will have all the trappings, all the dignity, all the solemnity, all the formalities, but after all, the board, with all respect to them, will be all dressed up and nowhere to go.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment is absolutely necessary in order that this court, so called, may be useful in connection with tariff matters. I want to point out to my right hon. friend that the court, as he himself said, makes no finding. The court makes no tariff, the court does nothing which

the ministry cannot correct if it pleases to correct it. So there can be no objection whatever to a man going before this court and saying: I want the facts investigated in this particular case. There is nothing binding on the government or on parliament, according to what my right hon. friend himself says about this court. But the amendment would give an opportunity for the public of this country to get information with regard to matters in connection with which they are paying money in the way of duties, paying money in the way of taxes and imposts, in order that they might see if those taxes were properly imposed. So I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment is one which should receive the commendation of this house. The comparison which my right hon. friend has made with the tariff advisory board has nothing whatever to do with the question. If he will say now that he will follow the same policy in the administration of this new board as was followed in connection with the tariff advisory board, he will go a long way towards meeting our views. But he has negatived that; he has said absolutely the reverse of that. He proposes to exercise jurisdiction in regard to this board just as the present Minister of Justice described it in 1912: It begins with the minister and ends with the minister. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that sort of board and that sort of court is not in keeping with the institutions of this country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Before the house rose last night I was protesting against the lack of information with respect to the various tariff items which are before the committee at this moment, also against the little time that is available by way of discussion of these amendments this session. I was pointing out that the proposed legislation we have before us is only part of the tariff changes the ministry has introduced since coming into office, and that it was understood at the close of the special session last year that full opportunity would be given at this session to discuss the tariff changes that were then made. Obviously that opportunity has not yet come, and I submit that at this late stage of the session it will not present itself. Similarly with regard to the proposed tariff changes, there has been no investigation before any body with respect to the items that, are going to be considered. In former years, as I pointed out, either a committee of the cabinet had held public hearings, or some board had listened to representations of different parties with respect to the effect of proposed changes, and the house had before it the printed evidence taken at those hearings as a guide to enable it to make up its mind as to what in the public interest should be done with respect to them.
I also took very strong exception to the extent of the changes in the tariff, both in range and in revision upwards, and pointed out as well the arbitrary manner in which all these changes have been made. They have not been made as the result of any investigation whatever, but simply at the instance of the Minister of Finance without hearings in the past as to their effect, and from what he has indicated on the tariff bill, without any possibility of future hearings as to their effects unless he so consents.
I desire further to point out in particular that these changes at this time are likely to emphasize the depression under which the country is labouring, and make relief from that depression infinitely more difficult and prolonged. The changes are all in the nature of further restrictions upon trade. In that regard they are in accord with the policy of the administration. I have said over and over again-and the Prime Minister has not denied it-that his policy with reirpect to these matters is to prevent coming into this
country all commodities which can be manufactured or produced in Canada. He believes that the ideal for Canada is to make of this country an economic unit which will produce and manufacture everything that is required for domestic consumption, and he hopes to effect that by putting up the tariff walls high enough to prevent importations from abroad.
That there may be no doubt about that being the point of view of the ministry-[DOT] though some of my hon. friends opposite seem to differ from their leader in that regard

may I quote a very definite statement made by the member of the administration who holds the portfolio of Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens)? Shortly after the administration came into office the hon. gentleman gave an interview in Vancouver to a representative of the Canadian Press, in the course of which he outlined the ideal of the administration of which he is a member. The despatch is dated Vancouver, August 31. and on September 1 appeared in the different papers of the country, including the Ottawa Citizen, from which I am quoting:
"The new government led by Hon. It. B. Bennett aims first to build up Canada industrially and agriculturally by suitable protective tariffs," said Hon. H. H. Stevens, who left for Ottawa to-day to attend the special session of parliament called for September 8. "Our ideal is that nothing hereafter will be imported except what cannot be grown or manufactured or otherwise produced at home."
Hear, hear.

And the Prime
Minister says "hear, hear."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That clinches the matter. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is further quoted as saying:
And if Canada cannot produce it, then we hope to get the goods from Britain or from our sister dominions.
May I again stress the quotation I have just read, and point out that the tariff changes which this committee is being called upon to consider at the moment have been made with the view of realizing the objective therein set forth. That, objective, of course, is what will

be accomplished if and when hon. gentlemen opposite have had sufficient time to complete their program; but the tariff changes as introduced at the special session and at this session go a long way towards helping them to reach their objective by the method that they at present are adopting. Let me repeat, in part, the minister's words which I have already quoted:
Our ideal is that nothing hereafter will be imported except what canot be grown or manufactured or otherwise produced at home.
Obviously the reason the administration has made these tariff changes as extensive and as high as it has is to further its policy of keeping out of Canada anything that can be produced or manufactured here. I wish to repeat that that is a policy of complete restriction of trade. If Canada is not to allow commodities to come in here from other countries, she cannot expect that other countries will purchase commodities from her. I need not go into the economic reasons why it is that in international exchange, imports ultimately must be paid for by exports, and that exports ultimately must be paid for by imports, but such is the undisputed fact; and I say that any policy which restricts trade to the extent of shutting off importations means that at the same time we are shutting off the possibility of exportations.
What necessarily is the effect of a policy of that kind? If effective at all, it will in a very short time bring about a condition of restriction of trade worse than any blockade in time of war. It will put an end completely to Canada's trade on the high seas, and will effect in a very material way our internal transportation as well I pointed out last night that for years past this parliament has been seeking to improve the means for facilitating international trade by making large expenditures on our railways and our harbours and subsidizing steamships, in fact improving transportation and communication in all its branches at great expense, all with a view of extending our trade internationally. Now an administration comes into office which definitely declares it is going to prevent commodities from coming into this country if similar commodities can be produced or manufactured here, knowing when it makes that declaration of policy that unless we are prepared to admit imports from other countries they in turn will shut out our exports to them. It is for that reason we take very strong issue with hon. gentlemen apposite in connection with these proposed tariff changes. If they become effective and serve the object which hon. gentlemen opposite have in view 
we believe they will bring about in this country a very serious condition of stagnation so far as trade and business are concerned.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have an entirely erroneous conception of the means of enlarging the home market which they say it is their objective to promote by their policies. If the home market were a given locality a place, however large, one could understand the desire to further the purchase and sale of all goods within Canada itself, but a market is not merely a place where goods are sold; it is a place also where goods are bought. Unless there is purchasing power the fact that you have a locality in which men meet to exchange money for goods will not affect the situation very much one way or the other. What is needed is purchasing power, and that purchasing power in Canada will come in very large measure through what in the export trade of this country is sold abroad. As we develop the great primary industries of Canada, agriculture, manufacturing, lumbering, fishing and mining; as we conduct a large export trade in connection with the products of these industries, so there will flow into Canada from abroad the purchasing power which is necessary to create a market for the commodities which are manufactured here. May I make this further statement with respect to manufacturing. Canada has now reached the point where she is exporting manufactured goods to a very considerable extent; if I am not mistaken she is at the present time per unit of population with the exception of Great Britain in manufactures the largest exporting country in the world. If that is the case and this policy is carried into effect, what is going to happen to our manufacturers? Our manufacturers will be obliged to lose their foreign markets and to that extent, along with other industries and business generally in the country, that particular interest will suffer very greatly.
What I want to point out particularly to my right hon. friend is this, that he himself has indicated to this house that to-day international competition is such throughout the world that a very slight difference in costs may mean insolvency to particular interests, or may mean the total loss of markets. In order that I ma.y do my right hon. friend no injustice I should like to quote his own words uttered in this house within the last two days. They appear in Hansard of July 7 at page 3473. At that time my right hon. friend said:
I have had some little experience in bus-ness; at one time it was rather extensive. I was privileged to have some knowledge of almost every branch of business, whether it was the packing business, the paper business,

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
the insurance business, the electrical business, or what it might be, and I realized that the question of cost was an all-important one, because even if your profit be only | of a cent per unit, if your volume is large enough you make an enormous fortune. I know of one case in which the profit on the single unit of production of the company amounted to less than | of a cent, and yet the volume was so large that the return was magnificent and it looked as though it were too large a return upon the investment. Yet the individual unit return was small.
That relates to the profit side; a very small margin, if spread over a wide enough field, may bring in a very considerable profit. But a little earlier my right hon. friend spoke about the possibility of loss, the effect of costs on markets together with their relation to competition, and I direct the attention of my right hon. friend and of the committee to these words as deserving the most careful thought and consideration. In order that their full emphasis may be appreciated I would point out that not only are costs of production and manufacture being increased by the very high tariffs created at the last special session and proposed in the resolutions before the committee at the moment; not only is the cost of living and the cost of production being greatly increased by virtue of the range and extent of increase in the changes which are being made, but there is being added to the taxation this year, for the first time, a one per cent excise tax on everything coming into Canada. That one per cent tax is over and above the customs duties, which are also in the nature of a tax, and I venture to say that the effect of these two things combined will be such that the costs of production with respect to almost everything, particularly when we have regard to the extent to which the cost of living will play its part in determining the wages item in cost of production as well, will be so great as to occasion many of those exporting concerns of to-day the complete loss of their markets abroad. Here are the words of my right hon. friend, also at page 3473 of Hansard:
Compare 1919 with 1931. I had occasion about a year and a half or two years ago to examine the cost sheets of a very large enterprise, and I was amazed to find that costs are no longer worked out in decimals of one-tenth of a cent, but down to four decimal places; that is, for example, to -8716 of a cent. In these days of modern competition the question of costs has become the all-important factor, and the costs director of a company is the man who very often determines its solvency or insolvency. When it is said that you can compare 1919 with 1931, no regard is paid to modern accountancy and to the relation which modern competition has created between the cost side of a business and its resultant product.
Think of the portent of that pronouncement. My right hon. friend, out of his own experience in business in this country, has realized that the difference of .8716 of a cent in cost may mean insolvency to a business which up to that time had been solvent. Here are changes in tariffs of not a fractional percentage but of many percentages, and an additional one per cent excise tax as well. Consider what these vast changes in tariff are going to mean when they are reflected in the production and manufacturing costs of the country. My right hon. friend says:
.... the costs director of a company is the man who very often determines its solvency or insolvency.
May I say that he to-day is the costs director, in his present position and with the powers he possesses, not merely of a company but of a nation, and in that position the costs director of a nation is the man who very often determines its solvency or insolvency. I am genuinely afraid that if my right hon. friend is permitted to continue with his tariff changes to the degree to which he proposes to go, and the further extent to which he may wish to go; if he is permitted to make still more rigid interpretations of existing legislation by orders in council, by special valuations, by bulletin appraisals and the like, conditions will become such that not for one industry alone but for many hundreds of industries there will be a difference in costs so appreciable as to change what is solvency to-day to insolvency tomorrow. That is my real objection to these changes as they are now proposed, and I think this of all times is the last moment at which experiments of this kind should be made.
May I say further that my right hon. friend is having considerable difficulty, in raising revenues. I do not think he has considered for one moment the revenue feature of the tariff which he has brought down. With discernment and care and previous investigation, he might have found means through the tariff of raising a very considerable amount of revenue. But in most cases he has put the tariff up to such a point that he has destroyed anything in the nature of a revenue producing feature. I think he himself will say that avowedly it is not tariff revenue he is considering at all; it is protection pure and simple, protection carried to the point of prohibition of all commodities coming into this country which can be produced or manufactured here.
Now, whatever views he may hold on that subject, I submit again that the present condition of the country should have caused the

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Prime Minister to move very cautiously in regard to the extent to which he would go in seeking at this time to put his views into practice.
The extent of the change which at this moment my right hon. friend is making in the tariff structure of Canada is the more surprising in that it runs directly opposite to the trend throughout the world which it is becoming more and more apparent will for the future be the prevailing one. It is true that immediately following the war there was In different countries a strong nationalistic development which asserted itself by way of increased tariffs and other forms of trade restriction. But the world has had a few years' experience of the consequence of that kind of policy, and the leading economists and many of the leading statesmen of the different countries of the world are to-day not only recognizing but asserting that unless the world can free itself from these nationalistic tendencies on the part of the nations there will be nothing but loss for all concerned. They are pointing out that what is needed to-day is not an endeavour on the part of different countries to raise tariffs to such a point as to invite further reprisals, but rather so to lower tariffs as to make possible more in the way of international exchange.
May I in passing direct the attention of the committee to the praise which has been bestowed upon the President of the United States for his action in suggesting a moratorium in regard to the payment of international debts between the different nations. IVhy have the countries joined in that great movement, and why has it been so universally applauded? The reason is that it removes one more restriction to international trade. It recognizes the desirability, not of purchasing everything within the confines of any particular country, but of enabling the nations to purchase one from another those things which each may have a comparative advantage in producing.
If that is sound doctrine with respect to a great movement such as that which the moratorium suggests in relation to international debts, I submit that the same reasoning will apply to other forms of restriction in trade. I wish to place before the committee two statements which seem to me to be most significant in this regard. They come from widely different sources but they represent that point of view which is being more generally entertained by those whose immediate concern is with large business.
The first statement was made by Sir Arthur Balfour, who in 1930 was chairman of the

British National Committee of the International Chamber of Commerce. Sir Arthur paid a visit to this country and he spoke in Winnipeg before the Canadian Club on April 23 of this year. I quote from the Canadian Press report as it appeared in the Gazette on the day following. These are his words:
"We have positively got to cease attempting to interfere with the laws of supply and demand," Sir Arthur Balfour, British industrialist and economist, said in an address today before the Canadian Club. "We have got to trade much more freely with one another if the world is to recover from its trade depression."
One of the greatest worries, said Sir Arthur, was that the agriculturist was receiving such low prices for his products, that he could not absorb the manufactured goods of the world. That was Canada's worry too.
"I think that tariffs have gone too far. They have their use arid place, but when they are applied to inefficient as well as efficient industries they go too far."
That is from a British industrialist who was chairman of the British National Committee of the International Chamber of Commerce, and it gives his considered opinion, reflecting the views of that body. The International Chamber of Commerce held a meeting in Washington this year, and there were presented to the president of that body representations from a newly formed Council for Tariff Reduction which has come into existence in the United States. It is the representative character of this new Council for Tariff Reduction and the very representative character of this International Chamber of Commerce that give great significance to the paragraphs I am about to read. I am quoting from the New York Times of May 7, 1931, an article which appears under this heading:
Drive To Cut Tariff Started Here To End World's Depression
Economists, Editors, Lawyers, Manufacturers and Many Other Leaders Back Plan Will Appeal to Congress Reduction in Armaments is Called Second to Ending of Port Barriers Letter Sent To M. Theunis Council for Tariff Reduction Puts Case Before the International Chamber of Commerce
The article reads:
The Council for Tariff Reduction is being formed by a number of prominent economists, editors, lawyers and manufacturers, it was announced here yesterday coincident with the sending of a letter by the newly organized body to Georges Theunis, president of the International Chamber of Commerce, now meeting in Washington, informing him of the belief of the members of the council that tariff walls must be lowered if world trade is to be revived.
Despite the unwillingness of the political parties to press for tariff reform at the coming session of congress, the council declared in its

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
letter to M. Theunis the intention of the new body is to press upon congress "the absolute need of prompt action at its approaching session in the reduction of the tariff of 1930, the ill effects of which have been immediately evident both within our borders and in international relations."
Among the prominent professors of economics who signed the letter and the announcement were Edwin R. A. Seligman, F. W. Taussig, David Saville Muzzey and Irving Fisher.
These names are all well known. Professor Taussig was a member of the tariff commission in the United States, and has been referred to by the present Prime Minister as the leading economist in that country to-day.

speechtext: One of the leading economists.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes; and I am proud to say that he was a professor of mine at Harvard while I was engaged in the study of economics. Perhaps I am reflecting some of his views at the moment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think they are becoming increasingly so. The letter sent to Mr. Theunis I shall now quote. And here I am attaching importance not merely to the source from which this communication comes, as representative of this council, and to the body to which it is addressed; I regard it as important also because of the views themselves and the appeal which they make to the minds of reasonable men who are thoughtfully studying conditions as they are in the world to-day. The letter reads:
In view of the advocacy of tariff reductions throughout the world by the International Chamber of Commerce at its previous meetings, and of your own address at the opening of the current sessions, you will be gratified to learn that there is in process of organization here a council for Tariff Reduction, which already includes several hundred leaders in economics, ethics, trade and industry. Despite the unwillingness of our political parties to face frankly within our own country this foremost world question, this council proposes to press upon the congress the_ absolute need of prompt action at its approaching session in the reduction of the tariff of 1930, the ill effects of which have been so immediately evident both within our borders and in international relations.
The council has not yet advanced its formal organization to the point of official expressions, but the attitudes stated in the correspondence of the members are definite. While it is generally recognized that the reduction of armaments, military, naval and aerial, is an urgent requirement to keep down national expenses and avert recurring deficits, our members realize that the lowering of tariff walls is the paramount necessity to permit economic laws to act in restoring world trade and national prosperity, a necessity pressing upon the several 22110-228
nations, and especially our own country, which has, unfortunately, led in tire enactment of skyscraping tariffs.
You may care to lay before the chamber or place upon its records the enclosed preliminary statement signed by the initiatory participants in the forming of the council. To these might be added the signatures of several hundred others, including many of the 1,028 economists who signed the protest to the president and the congress during the preparation of the Hawley-Smoot tariff
These signatures become the assurance that the opinions recently expressed in annual reports and public addresses by leaders in banking and industry have behind them the concurrence of an increasing number of our citizens, who recognize that to trade we must exchange and that to provide markets for our surplus manufactures, farm products, labour and capital we must be ready to remove the bars at our seaports which interfere so seriously with world trade. They are prepared to bring public opinion to bear upon our political leaders in favour of immediate tariff reduction and tliey_ desire to make known to those of liberal minds in other countries their sympathy and cooperation."
The statement of the organization of the council, with offices at 2 West Forty-fifth street, declared the tariff to be no longer a political, no longer merely a national, but a world-wide economic issue. It called attention to resentment engendered throughout the world by the Hawley-Smoot tariff, and declared that America, which has set the pace for high tariffs throughout the world, should now lead the way in tariff reduction.
Thus can our world market be extended, foreign customers increased, more home products demanded in exchange, unemployment decreased at home and abroad and a better home market developed through the increased purchasing power of our own workers in the wholesale round of economic progress promoting international goodwill and peace.
That statement, evidently most carefully prepared, sets forth as concisely and conclusively as any statement could, the argument for not increasing but decreasing tariffs if at the present time any change is to be made. I shall not repeat its arguments but allow the truth and force of them to speak for themselves.
May I conclude what I wish to say at this moment, by a further reference to the bearing of these tariff changes upon our own immediate pressing problem of unemployment? I feel that the government, by its action in making such extensive changes in the tariff, with their consequent trade restrictions, is pursuing a course which will not do other than increase unemployment. I know hon. members opposite sincerely believe their policies are going to result in stimulating manufactures and thereby increase employment. I am quite prepared to admit that at a certain stage of development in a country protection of a limited amount may under certain conditions with respect to particular

industries have that effect. But may I point out that Canada is at a stage of development very much beyond that of a country which is just beginning to take its place in manufacturing and in world commerce and competition. To-day the industrial life of this country is very widely and largely developed and there was not as recently as two years ago any pronounced demand even from the manufacturers themselves for further increases in the tariff. I venture to say that had it not been for the introduction of the Hawley-Smoot tariff bill, we would have heard practically nothing from Canadian manufacturers in the way of a demand for additional increases in tariffs. May I say this further:	I do not believe Canadian manufacturers have made any demand or request for the extensive increases in tariffs which are being proposed by the government. I believe they are in fact being greatly embarrassed by them.
May I repeat what I said the other day: In proposing tariffs as high as those which are before us in these resolutions, my right hon. friend is going directly opposite to what his predecessors in office of his own party always declared should govern in matters of protection in this country, namely: that it was not high tariffs; that it was adequate or moderate tariffs that were required, tariffs which would contain, if you like, the element of protection but certainly not tariffs which would go the length of prohibition. That is where I think my right hon. friend has made his mistake, and if instead of bringing forward of his own accord all these changes, he had in the first instance had his proposed changes carefully looked into and studied from the point of view not merely of the needs of the industry of the country but from the point of view of the incidence of taxation-where the ultimate burden of these duties is going to fall as respects industries and as respects consumers, and the effect of that upon the question of trade and unemployment in Canada at present-if he had done all these things, I believe he would have proceeded in a much more statesmanlike way, and at the same time in a way that would have served infinitely better to solve the great problem of unemployment, and to advance the interests of Canada, an end which at heart I know he desires to achieve.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

My right hon. friend

yesterday or to-day is any more forceful than what he said in the course of a two-hour speech a few days ago. Nor can it be said that what he stated on that occasion differs materially in its terms or substance from what he said on another occasion. It is his privilege to repeat these matters as frequently as he thinks desirable; for he must be given the widest latitude in the conduct of the fortunes of his party. He assumes the responsibility and he knows best what course to pursue in that regard. But may I remind him of just a few facts, the first being that we are confronted with conditions and not theories?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is what
I was saying.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: How is it working out?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I say that conditions
in the Dominion as a result of the action taken are better than in any other part of the world to which reference can be made. Outside of the fearful havoc that has been

wrought by conditions over which man has no control, no country is better situated than Canada to-day, and I say with some degree oi pardonable pride that had the action we took last September not been taken I do not know what would have been the result so far as industrial conditions in this country are concerned.
Let me proceed to the next proposal that I make. There never has been a time in the history of this country in which its industrial and manufacturing life was threatened as it is to-day, and by to-day I mean both the months that have just passed, the present, and the future that lies immediately before us.

What about
the country's agricultural industry?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I will come to that in
time. I have endeavoured up to the moment to indicate what the conditions were and the action that we have taken. We used tariffs, I said, to deal with one phase; we used dumping legislation to deal with another, in order to secure fairer competition. Then we dealt with the situation in a third manner, and this refers to agriculture as well as to ^manufacturing. It refers alike to manufactured products and to the products which the agriculturists of this country, through their organizations and societies, have asked us to protect and have sought from us legislation to that end, as I shall show as we go through the tariff schedules.
What did we do? We said that where you have goods coming into Canada at a price that makes it impossible for Canadians to compete, and where the dumping legislation is useless, we will confer upon the executive the power to place a price for duty purposes upon those products so that Canadians may still have fair competition and an equal opportunity. And we did that. We did it with respect to agricultural products. We did it with respect to fruits and vegetables. We did it with respect to dairy products, and with respect to every product of every kind that sought a market in Canada when we found that its admission to this market would destroy or seriously embarrass Canadian industry, be it agriculture or anything else. Under the circumstances those three measures were absolutely essential for the national life of Canada. I ask seriously: Will any hon. member of this committee say that under the conditions which he knows existed last fall the -whole industrial and agricultural structure of our life could have been saved had some action of that kind not been taken?
I think the right hon. gentleman has taken action which will destroy it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Having taken that action in the methods indicated, let us watch their operations. In a world of great depression we find that we are able at least to stimulate our industrial life and our national life, and we have improved agricultural conditions by giving to that industry some markets which it did not theretofore possess.
(Huron): Would my right hon. friend tell us what he 'has done?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
It is not a question of

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is my right
hon. friend always right?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No; I admit my own
fallibility, and before I have concluded I shall say more in that regard.
My right hon. friend has said that this session of parliament was called very late; it was. It was called four days later than the first parliament called by my right hon. friend in the year 1922.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, but that was within three not eight months of taking office. At that time there was only a moderate program of legislation, and there was no attempt to change the whole tariff.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
called ministers of experience; he had no change of governor general to contemplate, and there was no protracted vacancy of that office. As I have said, this session of parliament met at a date four days later than the first session of my right hon. friend after the year 1921. On that occasion Mr. Fielding delivered his budget speech on May 28; the budget speech of this administration was delivered on June 1. On the former occasion, however, the discussion did not last as long as it did at this session. There were no two-hour or four-hour speeches; there were no long reiterations of the same tale day after day, day after day. Those hon. members who care to look at Hansard will find there the evidence of what I now state.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will my right hon. friend tell me the number of tariff changes made in the budget of Mr. Fielding, and the number now proposed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As my right hon. friend

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On the contrary, there were very few.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We must remember also
that Mr. Fielding as a practical man clearly indicated then and later that faced with certain conditions he must apply practical means, not theories, and he proceeded so to do. As a result there was placed upon the statute books of Canada taxation with respect to stamps, with respect to cheques, with respect
to money orders, with respect to transportation, with respect to a sales tax which at one time was as high as 6 per cent and was 1: let-lowered to 5 and then to 4 per cent. He placed all these imposts upon the people, and did so because he was confronted with certain conditions. Being a practical man and applying a practical mind to the situation, he proceeded in the manner I have indicated.
To-day we are faced with what I conceive to be the most serious situation with which Canada has ever been confronted. Why? Because the depression has not been limited to Canada, but has been world-wide in its effects.
My right hon. friend admits that now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it has developed as I have indicated; there has been a gradual increase of depression.
That was not what my right hon. friend said last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
At that time it had not begun in some countries.
The depression to which I have referred being world-wide in character it followed that every country used its best endeavours to lessen it. That meant that every country was endeavouring to sell its surplus product to some other country in order that it might relieve its own financial situation. Canada retained its position among the nations of the world as the fifth greatest trading country. Canada's position however is more difficult than that of any other nation, for the simple and obvious reason that we live side by side with a nation of 120,000,000 people, separated from them by only an imaginary line, a people w'ho arc carrying on the greatest industrial development known to the world of to-day, and which has riches to compare with those of any other country in the world. What happened? For months and months and months they declined to release their inventories by selling at home at low prices, and sought a market in this country at almost any price they could secure. Let me illustrate. I have in mind competition which came not from that country but from a country across the water. The other day there came into my office the proprietor of a pin factory which has been doing business in the city of Montreal for thirty-five years and to a large extent supplying the entire requirements of this country. He had with him a small wire ring upon which were 144 safety pins of graduated sizes ranging in length from
