two inches to about a quarter of an inch. That ring of pins manufactured in Germany was actually being sold retail for five cents a ring.
Mr. McMILLAN (Huron).: Does not the Prime Minister think that the consumers of Canada would like to buy pins at that price?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I put this problem to the committee: Can you take the responsibility of saying that that small industry which had developed in thirty-five years to become one of a very substantial nature, giving employment to a substantial number of Canadians, should now be crushed and destroyed because of a world-wide depression which enabled a competitor to place 144 safety pins on the market for five cents.
We want to be practical, not theoretical. How many men did that industry employ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I understand upwards of fifty people.
Oh, oh.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member laughs -fifty people are nothing to him. But I say to him that I am concerned about the welfare of one Canadian.

Will my hon. friend
permit me?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not desire to be
further interrupted. Now, Mr. Chairman, I will mention another industry that employs very many more hands, amounting to hundreds. For instance, pianos are no longer sold to the extent they once were, because phonographs and radios to some extent have displaced those instruments; but they are still manufactured in this country in a small way compared with the extensive production that once prevailed in the industry. To-day because of the economic depression to which I have referred and the keen intent and purpose of other countries to sell their products within Canada, foreign manufacturers are offering grand pianos at $180. We cannot buy the wood to make them at that price. Are you prepared to destroy that industry or not? Yes or no. That is the question I had to answer, and you will find in the schedules the answer to it-I am not prepared to do it.
I will give another illustration. We have invested in this country millions of dollars in the radio industry, but that industry is small and insignificant compared with the 
industry in-shall we say-the great republic to the south. Their inventories were enormous. They had manufactured and manufactured and manufactured; and they looked and looked for a market. Then it became necessary to get any price they could to reduce their inventories. Is this country's radio industry to be destroyed for that purpose or not? That is the question. Take fruit. Last fall I stood on the road at a small junction point in British Columbia and saw seven carloads cf fruit that had just been brought in from Washington and Oregon. A few hours before I had been busy talking to those who have been trying to establish orchards in British Columbia and who are seeking only a fair return for their capital and labour. But they could not get a market for their fruit in competition with this imported product, because having obtained a high price for the requirements of their own people, the United States fruit growers had thrown their surplus upon the Canadian market to destroy Canadian fruit growers. Was that fruit growing industry a matter of importance to this country, or was it not? Was it important to develop in Canada a fruit growing industry, or was it not? Was it important that Canadians should or should not have fruit grown on their own land? That question had to be considered. It was considered. The answer was given in the seasonal tariff that wo passed last September.
Go down to the eastern townships and ask the people there with respect to the application of the same principle. Take butter- about which there has been so much talk. The price of butter has been reduced throughout the world, but we said when we were in opposition that butter was a commodity which should and could be produced by Canadians because it is a natural product of a country such as Canada. In days gone by Canadians were exporters of butter to the markets of the world. Then what happened? Because of short sighted action on the part of the government that industry was destroyed, and we became importers of the commodity to the extent of $9,000,000 from one country alone. Because we made that treaty with that result it followed of course that the inevitable would happen, and the Canadian people so influenced the mind of the government of the day that they gave notice terminating the treaty, with results that are well known.
Now, those are facts. I could give other illustrations. I could start with the lowest form of agriculture, the small truck garden on the outskirts of our cities, and trace the in-

dustry up through the larger garden to the orchard and describe the great industry that is involved in canning fruit and vegetables, and finally deal with the manufacturing industries of various kinds such as I have indicated. I aay that the government deliberately concluded that its duty was to pass such legislation as would prevent those who competed with us, whether they live far away or nearby, from destroying the national economic integrity of this country. By so doing we have added to the employment of our people; for every dollar's worth of goods brought in from abroad that might and could be made here, I repeat, means just that much less value in the way of work for a Canadian.

I wish the Prime
Minister could see the conditions in my own section.
Go behind a wailing wall somewhere.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is talking of the pulp and paper industry, over which this government could not have any control, this being an exporting industry. When we turn to our exports let us remember what they are and what they were. I took the trouble, just for my own satisfaction, to look at the figures. The agricultural and vegetable products of this country exported in
1929	represented a value of $255,307,675; in 1930, with decreased values, the exports of those products had fallen to $160,064,906-or a lessening of 37.2 per cent That was the net result of the depression to which I have referred and the reduction in value of our great grain products. The exports of animals and animal products decreased from $74,924,000 in 1929 to $52,779,000 in 1930, or 29 per cent. But during the first seven months of
1930	the exports of our wood and paper industry had decreased only to $150,000,000. The figure for the corresponding period in 1929 being $165,000,000. Then when the great overproduction of pulp and paper became apparent, through no fault of this government,-except with respect to one plant at least-because the provinces have sole control in regard to the matter, thousands of men who had looked to that industry for employment, small men who cut their pulp-wood and sold it to the mills-mills that no longer were occupied in producing paper; the cost of production, lowered though it was in every possible way, did not compensate in any sense for overproduction, and there was no demand either for pulp or paper or for
the pulpwood-those men found themselves without a livelihood, and so at once in Ontario and Quebec there was an increase^ of unemployment brought about by the creation of conditions over which the federal government, be it Liberal or Conservative, had no control. That is known to everyone. That is not a matter which touches upon our national life, except in so far as it touches upon our trade. I say to the right hon. gentleman that he must be aware of the fact that our exports-and I am coming to that phase of it in a moment,-are largely the natural products of this country, and in the very nature of things they comprise to a very considerable extent the raw materials of the industries of other countries. Look at the imports of paper into this country, made in many instances from our pulp.
What kind of paper?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Paper made from Canadian pulp in American mills for the production of Canadian magazines and farm journals. Does the hon. member want to know their names ? I shall be glad to give them to him privately at any time.

What are you going to
do about it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What we have already
done; we have passed legislation by which that drawback has been removed, and Canadian magazines and papers are being printed on the products of Canadian mills.

Do we produce the
magazines?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We produce the paper on which they are printed; that is what I am talking about. Does the hon. member forget what his Minister of Finance did with respect to a drawback on certain agricultural magazines?
I know exactly what was done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend
knows that the net result was to give business to American mills to provide paper for those magazines, and that has been done away with.
Are those mills still buying Canadian paper?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They are doing so
wherever possible, and before I finish I will come to that point. The necessity for other

countries to buy our raw materials ensures us a market. That is the position and will continue to be the position if we only observe the elementary rules with respect to the government of our own affairs.
Can they not get it anywhere else?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In many instances they cannot. I wonder if the hon. member does not know that Providence has been very kind to this country. We have more wonderful resources than almost any other country in the world. There are some forms of minerals necessary for the production of high class steel that can be obtained in this and no other country. It is tme that other countries have small deposits not easy of access, but these things have not yet come to light nor are they known to the commercial world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
When the committee
rose I had about concluded the statement I was making. But I desire to answer one question that was raised, namely, with respect to export or external trade. I pointed out that our exports had consisted largely of natural products, partly or wholly fabricated, such as vegetables, animal products, wood pulp and paper and non-ferrous metals. The statistics of the country establish clearly that we sell the commodities we do because people must have them; and that is borne out by the fact that our sales of paper in the neighbouring republic are not curtailed except to such a normal extent, in the absorption of newsprint, as one would expect under the present depressed conditions. Its entry is free, and the total decrease in sales for the first seven months of 1929 as compared with the first seven months of 1930 was 8-9 per cent. The decrease in non-ferrous metals, which are produced in abundance in this country and exported in the condition I have mentioned, was only 6-6 per cent. This shows clearly that where the requirements of other countries are as I have indicated, we are still selling our commodities to them. And these commodities, in the main, consist largely of paper and pulp and non-ferrous metals. This is abundantly established by the evidence we have before us. It is also true that in some instances our lumber sales have been taken 
from us in other countries by the lumber of our competitors, and we have been forced out of those markets. That arises from the very circumstances to which I have alluded.
A\ith respect to our export trade, it is idle for the right hon. gentleman opposite or anyone else to suggest that any government in Canada is not desirous of increasing that trade. But it might be well always to remember that every dollar of imports into this country represents, as I have said so often, the export trade of some other country; and to the extent to which we limit the export trade of another country into Canada, if we can supply the commodities ourselves, we enhance our own position. My hon. friend from Weyburn is constantly reminding us that tariffs can do nothing for agriculture-
Or anyone else.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. gentleman adds, "or anyone else." He is fair enough to make his statement universal in its application-that tariffs can be of no benefit to anyone at any time, ill any place or under any circumstances. The statement means, of course, that all the rest of the world is wrong and the hon. gentleman right, which I am sure must be gratifying to one possessed of such extensive knowledge.
And now may I make an observation with respect to the last statement of my right hon. friend opposite with reference to revenue tariffs. Henry George, in his book Protection and Free Trade, has something to say in this regard, and I could not help recalling it this afternoon If you are to have protection, he says, you cannot justify a revenue tariff under any circumstances; for if you believe in the principle you must apply it and not use it as excuse for raising a revenue. That, most economists are agreed, is but a subterfuge; it is nothing better than hypocrisy. Aou apply the principle of protection and then disclaim it, arguing that it results in revenue. As Mr. George points out, by extracts from others who hold similar views, that, is an unsound principle.
This can quite fairly be said with respect to agriculture: that while the wheat grower as such cannot reap benefits from tariffs, every small community in eastern Canada does, to the extent that industry may develop, creating a demand for the products of the farm.

speechtext: Do not forget'it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I shall not forget it, because it is the basis of the right of Canadians to live; it is the right they have. That right we shall protect. I might say, if I were so minded, in regard to the observations that were made this afternoon, that with respect to export trade, we considered the matter from the standpoint of another country. That in itself concedes the soundness of our position.. Go and ask any other country to give up part of its market to oblige the Dominion of Canada. Will it do so? Not one of them.
Is anybody asking us to do it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I oan say this: The only way in which that principle enunciated by the right hon. gentleman to-day can be carried out is just by doing that very thing. That is the difficulty in the world to-day. I have so often said that I am not tied to tariffs by any affection. Tariffs, I repeat, are merely the instruments that we use for our purposes, and as every other country is using them to the extent I indicated this afternoon, this .country cannot remain unprotected in a protected world. Everyone admits that. When I talk to my friends from the other side of the line, they at once admit the soundness of our position, namely, to care for Canada and protect it in the midlst of a protected world.
These schedules to which attention is now being directed we believe are prepared for the purpose of giving effect to the principles I have stated, and we have an assurance that prices will not rise by reason of their going into effect. We are confident, from our own experience and observation, that the competition which is created within our own borders will ensure us that measure of pricelowering which is essential for our development. Of that we feel certain. I cannot take time tonight, but I may do so before the session ends, to deal with some of the monstrously erroneous statements that have been made in connection with certain industries. In one instance it was indicated to the Canadian people that the loss by reason of prices which

it is said they had been compelled to pay on account of the tariff is greater than an entire year's revenue of the company affected. This is a small detail, but it is important to bear in mind how easy it is to dranv wrong conclusions from erroneous premises. I can only commend these schedules to the committee as an effort made by the government to advance the interests of the Canadian people as a whole, of agriculture, labour, the manufacturer, and every other interest within our borders.

I wish to protest on this
occasion against the cold indifference with which the Prime Minister views any efforts on the part of hon. gentlemen on this side of the house to secure information. The very day his budget was brought down I placed on the qrder paper a resolution asking for the production of the briefs and representations made by the publishers in regard to tariff matters. Expecting that I might be refused that information, I at the same time wrote a letter to the publishers themselves, asking them if they would furnish me with copies of their briefs and if they had any objection to my using them in public. I received a reply from them stating that their representations had been given to the government; that they did not feel justified in giving them to me without consulting the government, but that they had no objection whatever to the government giving them to me or making them public. Nevertheless, although we wanted this information at this time in order to discuss these items intelligently, we have not got it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I got the hon. gentleman's note after he had mentioned the question the other day. To what brief does he refer? The gentleman whom he mentions did not file a brief; he filed a short statement in connection with item 184 in the tariff schedules, the magazine schedule. I intended to ask my hon. friend just to what he did refer. I certainly did not quite understand him.

I have not seen all the
documents that have been filed. I understand they have filed certain documents asking for particular considerations, and I wanted to know what they were. The gentleman referred to in the letter did not feel justified in giving me any information in confidence, but he told me to apply to the Prime Minister and he would ask his principals if they had any objection to giving it.

to what document the hon. member refers.

If it is the one dealing with the magazine duties, the gentleman whose name he mentions in the letter is the one who saw me and gave me some memoranda with respect to the matter. If it is that-and I know of none other at the moment-there is no reason why the hon. gentleman may not peruse it as much as he likes. I have also the impression
they applied for certain things in regard to drawbacks; at least they were interested in drawbacks. I have not seen the documents, but I should like to get possession of them. I do not believe my right hon. friend is trying deliberately to keep us in the dark, but he has such a refined sense of honour in keeping things secret, I think he is overstraining it a little in not giving us information that would be really useful to us and that would not hurt anybody else if it were in our possession.
He told us this afternoon that when he came into power last fall unemployment was rampant in Canada. He did not say that it is better to-day, but he said that if we were in power, it would be still worse. I think he told the people he would end unemployment if he came into power.

speechtext: And he will.

We find that employment in June is lower than in May. In other words, unemployment is becoming worse instead of better in
spite of the new tariff launched last fall by my right hon. friend, a tariff which he seems to think has saved the country.
He said a short time ago that by lessening the trade of other countries with Canada we could improve our own position. I cannot understand the mentality of a man who takes that view. I cannot conceive how anybody can think that by injuring his neighbour he can help himself. Trade is exchange for mutual benefit. If it did not pay us to buy the goods of foreign countries, we would not buy them.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Is not home trade good too?
Yes, it is good, and if it did not pay us to buy home-made goods we would not buy them.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If two Canadians trade between themselves, then according to my hon. friend's theory, there are two profits for the two Canadians, but when a Canadian trades with an American there is only one profit. But apparently home trade does not matter to my hon. friend.
My hon. friend has heard of the jack-knife policy, where you trade your knife from one hand to the other, and expect to grow rich by so doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said that trade profits both parties to it, and I agree.

I say that we exchange goods for mutual benefit. When we buy goods from foreign countries it is because they have something which we want more than they do, and when we sell to foreign countries it is because they want our goods more than we do. We make an exchange and both parties benefit. My hon. friend asks why we should not exchange all our goods between ourselves. Why cannot we sell all our wheat to Canadians? Simply because they could not begin to buy it. That is why we have to buy goods from other countries if we wish to sell our goods to them, and when you shut foreign goods out of this country you are denying the whole of our exporters a market. How are we going to be paid for our wheat, our copper, our nickel, our pulpwood, our paper, if we do not accept foreign goods in exchange? The trouble in this country is that for the goods we export we cannot get much, and then when we buy goods from foreign countries the customs officer steps in and says that on the things that we are to receive in exchange for our wheat he will
3590	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
impose a duty of 25 or 35 or 40 or 50 per cent, as the case may be. When you shut goods out of this country you are simply saying to the exporters that they must take just that much less for their wheat, for their pulpwood, for their nickel, for their paper, and so on. How can anyone hope to benefit himself by adopting that dog-in-the-manger policy, by that beggar-my-neighbour policy, thinking he can benefit himself by hurting hi3 neighbour?
The right hon. the Prime Minister has admitted that this protective tariff could not be of much benefit to the wheat farmer, but, he said, in this budget he has given the farmer a compensating adjustment to the extent of five cents a bushel on his wheat. Up to when? While this adjustment is being made, while the home market is being developed sufficiently to take care of the farmers' products. And this adjustment is to last for one year! Does my right hon. friend really believe that by giving the farmers of the west five cents a bushel on their wheat for this year, we shall at the end of that period have developed our manufacturing industries in this country and increased our population sufficiently to absorb the entire wheat crop? Surely he cannot believe that. I pointed out on a former occasion that this five cents a bushel on wheat amounts to about eight per cent of the price of the farmers' wheat, but the exploitation that he is made to suffer because of this tariff amounts to about 30 per cent of his entire income. And we are offering him what? Five cents a bushel compensation for 30 per cent spoliation, and you call that a compensatory adjustment to the wheat farmer.
My right hon. friend mentioned a number of articles this afternoon to illustrate what he had done for the people of this country. In the first place he mentioned safety pins.
What does a bachelor want with safety pins?

Yes. My right hon. friend tells us that because somebody outside offered to sell safety pins in this country very cheaply he found it necessary to shut them out. I looked up the trade returns on pins, and I find that our import of pins last year amount to $128,000, on which a duty of $30,000 was paid. I could not find the domestic production, but looking up our exports I found that pins and needles were grouped together, and that we exported pins and needles to the amount of $502,000, and our imports amounted to $514,000. So our imports and exports substantially balanced. If we are

doing ourselves harm by buying pins from abroad, surely we are benefiting by selling pins abroad, and as I said, our imports and exports are about the same. But my right hon. Iriend is going to shut out this $128,000 worth of pins, and in doing so 'he is going to lose some $30,000 of revenue.
Hear, hear.

That is right. He tells us that by so doing he is going to keep in employment some fifty men. He could pretty nearly pay them their wages out of the revenue he is losing. I wonder if my right hon. friend has any idea how many women in this country, with children around them, find even such a cheap thing as pins very scarce and hard to get. It is all right for hon. gentlemen to laugh, but I know. Go into almost any house where there are children and you will find how scarce pins are. In order to carry out 'his policy, my right hon. friend will actually steal the pins from the little babies in the cradle.
My right hon. friend also spoke of what his government had done to encourage the piano industry in this country. He told us that the development of the radio and the phonograph had nearly ruined the market for pianos, that there was not much demand for pianos now, and the result was that other countries were offering to sell pianos in Canada cheaply, and he proposed to increase the duty to keep them out. Imports of pianos last year amounted to $288,000, and our exports to $218,000, so there is not very much difference. Here again my right hon. friend proposes to sacrifice revenue to the amount of $86,000 in order to encourage the making of pianos in Canada. Why are there not as many pianos sold in this country as formerly? Radio and the phonograph may account for it in part, but not entirely. There are thousands and thousands of people in this country who would buy a piano to-morrow if they could. WThy do they not do so? Because the price of a piano is just beyond their reach. It is for no other reason on earth. If my right hon. friend wants to create a market in Canada for pianos, let him bring down legislation that will bring the price of pianos within the reach of the people. Let him introduce legislation reducing the price of pianos, and immediately he will bring new buyers into the market for pianos, thereby increasing production and giving more employment. But by increasing the duty on pianos he puts them out of the reach of just so many more people, and ruins the market that he is trying to create.

My right hon. friend also spoke of book and magazine paper which he had shut out. I am speaking from memory, but I believe that the history of book paper coming into this country is this. It carried a certain rate of duty. Then some two or three years ago a rebate was granted to the Canadian publishers on book paper, printing ink, the machinery that they use, and generally on the articles that enter into their production. The result was that our Canadian publishers were able to effect a saving in the production of their magazines, which saving they put into improvements and betterments in the magazines. By improving their magazines they increased their sales to such an extent that they multiplied by three the amount of book paper which they required to use. in producing Canadian magazines. My right hon. friend told' us that our Canadian publishers must use Canadian paper. I understand that it actually costs the Canadian publisher 10 per cent more to print a magizine on Canadian-made paper than on American-made paper, because the Canadian-made paper is of inferior quality. So my right hon. friend is compelling the Canadian publishers not only to buy paper at a higher price, but also to use an inferior product which adds 10 per cent to the publishers' production costs.
My right hon. friend also spoke of certain metals which we have, and which no other country has, and he thinks we can force the rest of the world to buy them at our own price. Let us take nickel, for example, which possibly my right hon. friend had in mind at the time. We own So per cent of the world's nickel.
Ninety per cent.

All right; we will say ninety per cent. We can more than supply the entire world demand for nickel. The development of the nickel industry in Canada has reached the point where it is necessary not only to supply the present market but to create a larger one. The. problem confronting nickel companies to-day-and I think hon. gentlemen opposite will agree-is how to find new uses for their product.
How about a five cent piece?

They have to find new uses- and in answer to my hon. friend I will say the five cent piece is to be given to the wheat farmer. If the policy of my right hon.- friend is carried out, the cost of producing nickel will be increased, the cost on the world's market will be increased and the use of that commodity will be thereby limited.
How does he do that, if he adopts the reverse policy?

If the reverse policy is adopted nickel will come into use for different things; more buyers will come into our markets; there will be a greater demand for nickel; there will be more men employed in its production, its refining, its transportation, and thus many other industries will be assisted.
Rot.

It is not rot-these are actual facts. However sincere my right hon. friend may be, his policy is having the very reverse effect. The other night I tried to explain that the production of manufactured goods per capita is much greater measured in dollars and cents than the production of primary products per Capita. When manufactured goods are shut out to the extent my hon. Mend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) would sugest, namely $800,000,000 a year, you are shutting out goods and creating employment for 147,000 men, who will be required to produce those goods at home, but. you would be throwing out of employment twice that many men because those $800,000,000 worth of imports must be paid for by $800,000,000 worth of exports. Those exports would be of primary products the .production of which requires twice as many men as the production of manufactured lines. Therefore by increasing the prices in this country my hon. friend's policy is bound to restrict still further the buying power of the people, cause a further slackening up of business, and create more instead of less unemployment.
Will the Prime Minister assure this committee that he will alpply impartially to all branches of Canadian industry the policies he has so often emphatically announced to this assembly?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: So far as it is possible to do so, he will.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to submit a question to the Minister of Finance, and I hope he will answer it more fully than he answered a question I directed to him a few days ago. I am sure he must have known that his reply at that time did not constitute an answer at all.
He has repeatedly stated, and said again tonight, that he wants such a tariff as will give a fair opportunity and ensure equal competition to Canadians. When I spoke on the budget I said that I had no fault to find with that kind of tariff. On that occasion I stated

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
that the Prime Minister had repeatedly expressed his desire to have such a tariff as would ensure that all commodities possible of production in Canada would be made in Canada. If I am misquoting him I should be pleased to be corrected, because I find a difficulty in reconciling those two principles. I should like to ask the Prime Minister to make an explanation, because if he enacts such a tariff as will provide fair competition and give an equal opportunity to Canadians, he does not imply exclusion. If there is competition at all, goods must be coming into the country; if it were not so there could be no competition whatsoever. To my mind such a condition does not agree with his other principle, namely the imposition of a tariff which will shut out such goods as can be produced in Canada. I am honestly asking for information on this point and I would appreciate an attempt on the part of the Prime Minister to reconcile those statements and make his position clear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I remind my hon.
friend (Mr. Euler) that I said all the Canadian required was an equal opportunity and fair competition, and I added, as has been my habit, that no Canadian asks more, if he is certain that he will at least have a market for his product.

Does my right hon. friend
think that that necessarily follows?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. Give any Canadian an equal chance with his competitor; give him fair competition, as distinguished from unfair, and he will get the business.
All the business?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He may not get it all,
but he will get all he wants. The reasons are quite obvious. I have said nothing about prohibitions, but did say I was anxious that the Canadian should manufacture everything he required if it could be produced in this country under conditions of fair competition and equal opportunity. To do more than that might mean on the one hand exploitation and on the other hand putting a premium on inefficiency. If you gave him less, it would be unfair; if you gave him more, you would be placing a premium on inefficiency. Unfairness and destruction would result in the first case and exploitation in the latter.

I thank my right hon. friend for the explanation he has given, but I think he will find, as most business men admit, that where there is equal opportunity and fair competition both competitors will sell some

goods. I am not objecting to that, but I think the inference thrown out by the Prime Minister that if the Canadian ha3 an equal opportunity he will get all the business is perhaps a little more complimentary to Canadians than I -would care to oe,-and at that I have a veiy good opinion of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, as no item has been called this would appear to be a sort of supplementary budget debate. I am not going to prolong it, but I lliink it has some value inasmuch as at least it gives us an opportunity of understanding each other's viewpoints. We look upon the protection policy of our hon. friends opposite- especially their efforts of last fall-as something in the nature of a disease which will have to run its course before any remedy can be effected. My hon. friends opposite look upon low tariff men or no tariff men as those afflicted with another sort of disease. If at least we can reach the point where we respect, each other's viewpoints the present discussion will not have been without some purpose.
May I point out to the Prime Minister that it is one thing to put up a tariff such as that of last fall, especially on farm implements, and it is quite another thing to make the farmers buy those implements, to buy implements they do not want to buy, or to use implements which they find are not best adapted for their particular purposes. Purely the Prime Minister remembers the reciprocity struggle and the bitterly disappointing effect it had on the farmers in the west. Although the reciprocity pact provided for a lowering of tariffs, western farmers were so disappointed because of losing the American market for their farm produce that many of them deliberately bought more farm machinery from the United States than they had ever done before. That may have been shortsighted, it may have been in some cases foolish, but it was very natural.
I do not think however that the experience at the time of the reciprocity pact will be repeated on this occasion. I have two reasons for making that statement. Although the tariff has gone up tremendously and we do not know where it will end, I do not think that the tendency to buy more farm machinery from the United States will grow. In the first place just now, the farmers have nothing to buy with; their purchasing power is lower than I have ever known it to be. They are tinkering up their old harness, patching up their machinery and making it operate as long as they can. If the tendency to which I referred does not revive-that is the buying

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
of more American farm machinery, no thanks are due to this government because they have done everything in their power to encourage it. But it will not be done for another reason. During the eight or nine years that the King government was in power we believe our gradual reduction of duties all along the line-increasing the British preference and decreasing the duties on farm equipment and many other commodities-had the effect of promoting a better feeling 'between the west and the east, particularly between our western farmers and our eastern manufacturers. I wonder if anybody will deny that? That good feeling still largely prevails unless my hon. friends opposite have already driven it away entirely by their tariff policy. But, as I said before, no thanks to this government. They are inviting the west almost to do it, and when we think of the other things that the government have done,, especially to the wheat pool, it will be surprising if there is not resentment shown in that or some other way-possibly by the ballot. I suggest to my hon. friends opposite their oareful consideration of what I have stated before they go too far with their high tariff policy-they have gone pretty far already.
Since the Prime Minister has referred to butter, let me also refer to it. Why did he double the duty on butter that the farmers themselves asked for? The national dairy council asked for a duty of only four cents a pound when they appeared before the tariff board, and they got it. On more than one occasion in my presence they were advised by the late hon. Mr. Robb to take their case before the board. They dlid not do so at the time because they felt they had not sufficient evidence to justify an application; later on they presented their case fior a four cent tariff, and, as I have said, their request was conceded at once by the tariff board. That was all the protection they wanted, and yet my right hon. friend went twice as high- he placed the duty at eight cents. I wonder if that is what he did with the manufacturers? When our administration w'ent out of office I did not know any manufacturer who wanted a higher tariff. I was not around the year before, and they may have come bo the government for higher protection, but I do not think they did. If the present government dealt with the manufacturers as they did with the dairymen, then they must have given them twice as much as they wanted. That is what, we object to. We should like to know why the government did it. Perhaps the Prime Minister will tell us now why he gave the dairymen twice as much duty on butter as they asked for. The dairymen actually
objected to that duty of eight cents per pound. If the right hon. gentleman carries out that ,policy all along the line in connection with other commodities, he might tell us so. We have been criticized for adopting a tariff for a revenue, because such a tariff embodies a certain amount of protection.
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
When asked in a nice way like that, certainly.

What duty did the
Dunning budget impose on butter?
Four cents.
Against the United States?

countervailing duty was.
It was twelve cents.

speechtext: I hardly think that would be in order on this section.

That is the amendment 1
intend to move. During t'he discussion the Prime Minister accepted the amendment at one stage

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps it would assist
the hon. gentleman if I were to say that we will let section 17 stand, because in any event it involves the numbering of the sections that are dealt with. While I think the hon. member is not strictly in order in proposing his amendment to this section, he might proceed if he wishes to do so, though it will be observed that in subsection 2 the various items dealt with are mentioned, and we will leave -that in the event of some of them being slightly changed.
I did not exactly understand what the hon. gentleman was proposing. Had it something to do with the unions?

Did I understand the
Prime Minister to say we might proceed with this discussion now? I will not detain the committee at any great length. In 1930, during the special session, I had the honour of proposing practically the same amendment,
and the Prime Minister stated that he saw no reason why it should not be accepted after some changes were made in the phraseology A little later in the discussion the Prime Minister thought it would be reasonable if we left this matter over until this session, when we would be dealing with the whole tariff. This is the first opportunity we have had since that time, and consequently I offer this as a suggestion to the government,.
I do hope the Prime Minister will take this opportunity of seeing to it that these industries which are protected by the people of Canada will be forced to treat their employees properly. I realize that there are different scales of wages in different parts of the country, and that different hours of labour are maintained in different industries and different localities, but the Prime Minister says it is wrong in many ways to have unfair competition from other parts of the world. It is equally unfair that industries in certain parts of this country =hould have an advantage over industries in other parts, through a different in the treatment accorded to the empllo3rees. I have in mind at the moment the province of British Columbia, where they have a minimum rate of wages for workmen in all industries and where they have the eight horn- day. Yet we have industries in other parts of the country that will not pay a decent wage and that are *working their employees long hours. It is just as bad for an industry in one part of the country to treat its employees unjustly as it is for one country to treat its citizens unjustly.
In addition, as has been stated, we are a party to the treaty of Versailles, to which we have affixed our signature. One of the provisions of the treaty of Versailles, with the conventions arising out of it, was that we should adopt an eight -hour day. I had thought until last session that this was purely a provincial responsibility; I had never dreamed of associating it with tariff measures. But the present Prime Minister and some of his colleagues showed how it could be carried into effect by making it obligatory on the part of those industries that are receiving protection from federal legislation to apply the principle in their operations. If I recall rightly, the Prime Minister at the time twitted me, as Minister of Labour, for not taking part in the discussion. I may confess that I could not take part in the discussion because I was bewildered. For many years I had been led to think that questions of hours and wages were provincial responsibilities, and I could not understand all at once how the principle

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
could be made to apply in connection with federal legislation with respect to the tariff. So that I could not take part in the discussion under those circumstances. But I agreed with what the Prime Minister, at that time leader of the opposition, said, speaking from this side of the house.
This matter has now been two years before the house. I submit that it will not work hardship on any industry which is treating its employees fairly to have this principle recognized, and it will in a measure equalize the conditions that obtain in industry throughout Canada. I make this suggestion in the hope that the government will now accede to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is obvious that the hon. gentleman's reason for not engaging in the discussion to which he refers was not that he was bewildered at what had been suggested; it was his long attachment to the administration with which he was associated. However, I can only say, with reference, to the measure which we have just passed, that we have endeavoured to meet the situation under the tariff board. It would be idle to add the provision to the customs tariff without having some machinery whereby the facts might be ascertained; and as the law now stands direction will be given to have inquiry made. The hon. gentleman himself will be the first to realize that no action could be taken unless an inquiry were made. Any action taken would have to be based upon the findings of that inquiry. Knowing that the hon. gentleman and the hon. member for AVinniipeg North Centre would have something to say about the matter, I did give it consideration, and I say again that the provisions under the tariff board with respect to inquiries meet, in our judgment, the case that has been indicated.

The statement of
the Prime Minister is satisfactory only in part. We took the matter up the other day when the section in the tariff board bill relative to this subject was under discussion. In so far as provision is made for inquiries, that would seem to me to be satisfactory. But I note that in clause 17 now before us the Prime Minister is attempting to safeguard the consumer. Conceivably, clause 17 might not be necessary in view of the tariff board regulations as they were expounded to us the other day. Yet that clause appears in this measure, definitely providing that if any producers take advantage of the tariff to maintain prices at levels which the governor general in council deem to be higher than are warranted, then the protection may be removed. As I understand the remarks of

the hon. member (Mr. Heenan), he . is arguing that similar provision should be made with respect to the employees. If it is necessary in this legislation to insert a clause providing for the protection of consumers, it does not seem unreasonable to ask that the protection to be accorded to the employees should be definitely and explicitly stated. I have all along maintained that so-called protection of industries was no guarantee that the workers in industry would be protected, and it seems to me that if the Prime Minister is in earnest in his desire to protect Canadians-he has so frequently said that Canadians must be protected-there is no reason why, definitely and explicitly, Canadian employees should not be protected and provision be made guaranteeing that protection. We have machinery for inquiry, but we have no guarantee whatever that if wages are found to be insufficient, or if working conditions are not desirable, there will be any action to redress these conditions. It would seem to me that if this matter were entrusted to the governor in council and if it *were stated definitely that, should the general conditions of labour not comply with a certain standard, then the protection shall be removed, that would give us something to work upon. The Prime Minister himself made a clear-cut Statement in this regard when the steel schedules were being discussed a year ago. In fact, it was he himself who suggested a clause of this kind. He said that if a year went by and changes were not made he would see, if he were returned to power, that such provision would be made. As a matter of fact on!)' modified changes have been made. In one of the factories under discussion the men, it is true, are not working eleven and thirteen hours they are working, some of them, ten hours. They should be working only eight hours. I have no information as to whether the hours have been reduced in the other factory in Algoma. I submit that the principles which were enunciated at that time by the Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, apply to-day, especially now that the right hon. gentleman has the power in his own hands. I urge him to . insert such a clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Clause 17 is not the
appropriate place to take it up. I suggest that 17 be passed, the hon. gentleman reserving his right to take the matter up again by way of amendment or otherwise. I will afford him facilities for discussing it.

The Prime Minister's
suggestion that the bill already passed provides for an inquiry of this kind is futile in con-

nection with this tariff, because this tariff has been made without the intervention of the tariff board. It is not likely that there will be any inquiry on the part of the tariff board so far as these particular items now before us are concerned. The Prime Minister suggests that there is no machinery. As I understand the matter, the amendment suggested by the hon.' member for Kenora-Rainy River is that the governor in council shall have power to make an inquiry or shall make an inquiry, and there is sufficient provision in the Inquiries Act for that purpose.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who has jusft Spoken will perhaps realize that many of the applications now being made to the United States board are for reductions, and reference of particular items has been made to that board notwithstanding the fact that the tariff items were adopted by congress and approved by the president about a year ago. I say that for this reason: I do not know whether the hon. gentleman was in the chamber or not all the time that I was speaking this afternoon, but I endeavoured to suggest -and I think my suggestion is warranted by the facts-that an emergency condition such as now prevails is the justification for the action that was taken; that in some instances mere tariffs are not ample for the purpose, and that, in order to cover the situation regard must be had to the third measure that I mentioned, namely, the fixing of a price for duty purposes. I can assure the hon. gentleman that I contemplate that the Minister of Finance of the day will frequently refer matters of this kind to the tariff board-
He may.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; I give it as my
opinion that he frequently will do so for the purpose of ascertaining just what the President of the United States has been able to ascertain recently in connection with several matters when the duty has been reduced all the way from 4 to 50 per cent. That at any rate is my hope.
That is only the exception rather than the rule.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is true.

I do not want to indulge
in political talk or I could very well quote
what some hon. members on the other side said, indicating the enthusiasm they displayed in connection with this very same matter in the regular session of 1930. I remember quite well some of the present ministers of the government then taking the position that we could say to the industries: Yes, we shall give you protection provided you protect the workingman of the country, and only on that condition. Their enthusiasm seems to have died down since that time. I do not, however, want to go into that. I would much rather let the government or any party take the credit of doing what I wish, so long as it is done. We have in Canada industries-and I have experienced this myself-that will not permit their men, under penalty of dismissal, to join a labour organization, and this notwithstanding the fact that Sir Robert Borden on behalf of the Dominion of Canada appended his signature to the Treaty of Versailles giving these men freedom of association. We have United States companies establishing industries in this country and telling our Canadian workmen: No matter what the laws of your country are; no matter what the treaty of Versailles has to do with the matter, we are going to run this industry and you will work the hours we proclaim or you will leave this job. I think the Prime Minister himself would be the first to say that it is not fair for one industry in a province to make its employees work ten hours a day while another industry of a similar character in * the same province is making its employees work eight hours a day. I do not think that is fair. The proposal that I make is not ambiguous. It says simply: '
The governor in council may direct from time to time that any industry, the products of which receive protection under this act, shall demonstrate to the satisfaction of the governor in council that freedom of association for employees for all lawful purposes is permitted in the operation of such industry.
All the government has to do is to ask the industry if they are allowing their employees the right to organize. If we had something like this, we would not be confronted rvith what I was up against when I was Minister of Labour, because I had nothing back of me except that I could say that Canada was a signatory to the Peace treaty. I had no law, not a sentence in the whole of Canada that I could find, to say to employers of labour that they should maintain freedom of association. If we had a clause like this in the tariff legislation, the Minister of Labour or the Prime Minister could say to those concerns that are discriminating against their employees: This is the law of Canada, and if you will not abide by

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
the laws of this country, we shall have to-take other steps to see that you do. This is all this clause will do, and I think if the Prime Minister will only consider my amendment, he will accept it.
I understand the hon. member is not pressing this as an amendment to section 17, but submitting it as section 18, an additional section.
I want to insert it where the Prime Minister thinks suitable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will perhaps recall the language of the then Prime Minister after he had taken time to confer with his legal advisers as to what the position was. Only the other day I had this matter looked into. The judgment of the privy council which stated that this parliament had acted ultra vires in declaring that to solicit insurance under certain circumstances was a criminal offence, and which carries the law to an extent that had not formerly been thought possible, has been looked upon by some as indicating that that power to solicit exists. I am bound to say I thought the difficulty the then Prime Minister pointed out was leas than subsequent investigation would indicate would be the case.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that is perfectly frank, for you cannot single out a particular industry.
The difficulty has become more weighty now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Well, the then Prime Minister had the advice of the Minister of Justice at that time, and I have the same. The hon. gentleman will find that you cannot select one particular industry. I have endeavoured under section 17 to provide for the selection of an industry, that is one of many that is exploiting the consumer. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth expressed some doubt about the value of the section. All I am endeavouring to do is to say that quantum valeat, for what it is worth, we are endeavouring to enact it.

Whatever difficulty may have prevailed last year when a particular industry, that is the steel industry, was singled out, would not prevail in the insertion of a clause of this character in the schedule.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it would.

This would apply
generally.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The difficulty is of industries being in different provinces. The hon. member pointed it out frankly a moment ago, but perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did not hear him. The difficulty was in applying it and the method by which it could be enforced.

It still remains true that if special consideration is given to any industry, whether located in British Columbia alone or in all the provinces, this is a special grant by the Dominion government or by the people of Canada, and the government has a perfect right to state the' conditions under which the grant shall be given. I think that is true.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is not a grant.

We would be laying down a general rule that would provide if any industry were seeking in any way to obtain special consideration from the government- and I do not think the leader of the opposition would say there is anything in the constitution to prevent a general provision of this kind-the Dominion government is competent to determine the conditions which must prevail. The government is already taking that power with regard to the fixing of (he price of goods. If they are fixed too high, the government says they must be reduced or else the special privilege will be withdrawn. If the Dominion parliament has authority to do that, it has also authority to impose other conditions; all I plead for is that in making the general provisions the working men be not left out. Clauses protecting him ought to be as explicit as the provisions with regard to the protection of the consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend does not realize that the matter of imports into Canada is one that comes especially under the jurisdiction of this parliament. The levy of a customs duty is not in the nature of a grant in any way, shape or form. It is a provision under which goods are admitted into this country, and the fixing of prices, which my hon. friend mentioned, is not the fixing of the price at which goods shall be sold in various provinces of Canada, but the fixing of a price at which they shall be valued for the purposes of customs duties. The difficulty in regard to hours of labour, joining associations and matters of that kind, is that these are not matters over which this parliament has any control or jurisdiction. If it were a money grant 1 assume conditions could

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
be attached, but it is not a money grant. It is a matter affecting imports into this country, which is especially placed under the jurisdiction of the Dominion authority.

The hon. member for Bow River said the other day that he noticed that sometimes lawyers disagreed. That was a revelation to me. I always thought that they agreed. The present Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition in 1930 said that we had the power to attach conditions. He said, at page 2374, of Hansard of May 21, 1930:
I confess, Mr. Chairman, that there is only one question in my mind: Have we the power? The answer must be in the affirmative. Having the power, then should we not exercise it? I put that to my hon. friends opposite, because here we have no division of opinion; we are all committed to it.
After the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition talked the matter over they decided that it had better stand over to a later date, when they might apply that provision to all the tariff measures. I remember that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked the present Prime Minister if he would support a move along that line at a, later date, and at. page 2740 of Hansard of that date the present Prime Minister said:
The question is not an unfair one, and I have no hesitancy in saying that unless a reasonable excuse is offered I propose to do so.
I could quote from several other hon. gentlemen who took the position that we ought not to grant either a bonus or tariff protection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was a bounty in that case.
I know it was a bounty, but it is the same thing as a bonus.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A bounty is in the nature of a grant, and when we make a grant we can attach conditions.

I was coming to that. I
heard someone behind the minister whispering that it was a bounty that was being dealt with at that time. I say that we were not dealing with a bounty at that time, but with a. tariff measure. The trend of the whole debate in 1930 was that we could attach any conditions we liked with respect to any industry that was given tariff protection. I believed then that we could, and I believe so now. If we do not do it, it is because we have not the wish to do it.

I fail altogether
to follow the argument of the Minister of Justice. Let me read section 17.
In the event of producers of goods taking advantage of any duty imposed under this act to increase the price of such goods to the consumer-
I ask, what producers? The Minister of Justice would seem to imply that it is producers in the United States or in Belgium or in some other foreign country. If his argument is worth anything it must be producers outside Canada, but as a matter of fact the producers which this clause lias iu view are the producers here in Canada, the producers of competitive goods produced in Canada, and if the producer in Canada takes advantage of his opportunity to raise the price above the level that is deemed proper, then the governor in council may act. I submit that the proposal made by the hon. member for Keaora-Rainy River is in principle very similar to this. If the producers in Canada undertake to produce goods under unfair conditions the governor in council shall have the right to cancel the tariff privileges that are being granted. Now if we have the right to cut down the price, of goods, I think we have also the right to protect the people who are engaged in making them. It seems to me that the principle is the same, and I would hope that the Prime Minister would see the necessity of protecting the large body of workers who are involved in a matter of this kind. He has so definitely and emphatically stated that the idea underlying the government's tariff policy is to protect Canadians that I cannot understand why he should refuse to undertake definitely to protect that large body of Canadians known as labour men.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Surely the hon. gentleman realizes just what the issue is. He certainly has beclouded it. Last year the issue was the question of a bounty, the grant of a sum of money, and I expressed certain opinions with respect to it. To-day the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River endeavours to say that the governor in council can deal with specific industries. There are in this country, we will say, nine industries in nine provinces. In four of them every detail of the treaty of Versailles is observed; in the other five it is not. What are you going to do ahout it? That was a different case altogether from the one before us. In that case a bounty was given to an industry. There is an additional reason why you could not attach any such provision here. The

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
defence of anyone affected would be that he was complying-with the laws of the province, and that the province has complete control, as the supreme court said.
Might I ask if the right hon. gentleman considers that an adequate defence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is a complete legal
defence, because this is not a grant.
It is not a money grant, I will admit, but is it not the grant of a certain privilege? I shall not call it a special privilege if the Prime Minister objects to that phrase.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not a privilege. If there are nine industries, one in each province, and in four every rule and regulation of the treaty of Versailles is observed, how can we deal with the other five?

On that very same basis, on the ground that the industry is asking for a " special favour," if I may use that phrase, although I will put a question mark after it if the Prime Minister prefers. Here is a certain concession which this industry is seeking. I would say that the general provision should be that all industries benefited must live up to the requirements of the Versailles treaty. It does not make any difference if only some of them are living up to it. We simply maintain the position that no one can have this privilege unless he lives up to the treaty.

It is not a favour that
we are asking, but a favour that the government is giving to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that would be about the correct figure.

This increase means an
additional tax of something like $140,000. Already the price has been raised. I have received information from one of the leading centres in the province of Nova Scotia to the effect that a farmer who has been paying $26 to S27 a ton for barley and $25 to $26 a ton for corn was quoted new prices, just after the bringing down of the budget, of $31 for barley and $32 for corn. I can only say that this is a very heavy tax on the primary producers in the maritime provinces. I think the suggestion is that possibly they may be able to use some other feed. My information is that barley cannot be used for the purposes for which they are using corn, particularly in connection with feeding poultry.

The corn used is
mostly Canadian.

A good deal of corn is imported from the Argentine. I do not think this is a very good beginning in view of the mission we sent to Argentina for the purpose of promoting closer trade arrangements with that country. I understood from the newspaper reports that there had been an extremely fine reception given to the Canadian representatives. I read in the Free Lance of Pictou, a newspaper published by one of the gentlemen who was a member of the delegation from Canada that:
He had had conferences with gentlemen holding high places in the governments of the Argentine and Brazil in regard to closer trade arrangements, and in both instances he was accorded a joyous welcome and given assurances that closer trade arrangements with Canada *would find them ready at the halfway mark to deal in a sympathetic way with proposals form the Canadian government.
Nova Scotia sells fish and coal to the Argentine. This affects Nova Scotia particularly. My right hon. friend is not only

shutting off that trade with the Argentine and making it more difficult for us to sell pur fish and coal there, but at the same time he is imposing a heavy tax of 20 cents a bushel on the feed used by our farmers.
Is it not admitted that the coarse grains of the west are equally as good as corn for all purposes, with the exception of poultry feeding and starch making?
My information is that barley is not nearly as satisfactory as corn for the particular purposes for which our farmers down there use it.
Is that limited to poultry feeding?
They simply have to pay the additional tax.

I rise, Mr. Chairman, to protest against the duty on corn. I am afraid this is going to be a great blow to the poultrymen of British Columbia. We of British Columbia, particularly on the Pacific slope, are peculiarly situated in that we are far removed from the grain fields, and we have great areas of land not adapted to general agriculture. We, have the climate, however, and the soil is well adapted to the raising of poultry and small fruits. I do not believe any other province has specialized in the poultry industry to such . an extent as has British Columbia. Ours is the only province that has gone into the poultry industry in a large way. Really it has become an industry pretty much along the same specialized lines as a manufacturing plant. Our poultrymen have specialized to such an extent that to-day British Columbia hold the highest records for egg production in Canada. But the poultrymen of British Columbia have to purchase all their grain from practically outside sources. As I say, the British Columbia poultry plants can be considered as being something like manufacturing plants

men go into the business with the sole object of producing eggs and poultry as a means of livelihood. This tariff tax is going to be an added cost on our production and we are now faced with a very serious state of affairs indeed. I believe I am right when I say some of our grain merchants have increased the cost of corn already. However, this duty will mean a difference of about fifty cents a sack or nine dollars per ton. I have heard it said in this house by many members that barley is as good a feed as corn for poultry. I hold in my hand the latest bulletin issued by the Department of Agriculture under the authority of the minister (Mr. Weir),.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
entitled Canadian Grown Grains in Poultry Feeding. I am going to deal with only one or two items in this bulletin in an endeavour to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister that barley cannot be substituted for corn for poultry feeding. There is no one grain adapted for the production of eggs; we must have a variety of grains, and barley cannot be wholly substituted for corn. To begin with barley is not as palatable as corn, and it contains much more fibre. Barley is deficient in what is known as vitamin A. This bulletin says:
In so far as vitamins are concerned all four grains are good sources of vitamin B, considering this to be the antineuritic vitamin the presence of which prevents the occurrence of a deficiency disease known as polyneuritis in fowl, and corn is the only one which contains the growth-producing antiophthalmic vitamin A, which is of importance in poultry work particularly where growing stock is concerned and in the prevention of ophthalmia, a deficiency eye disease not uncommon to poultry.
According to the chemical analysis-and here may I point out for the benefit of the Minister of Agriculture that it seems strange to me that we have to go across the line to get an analysis of our grains, as in this bulletin the analysis is taken from a United States bulletin-I find the chemical analysis shows that the fibre content of barley is just double that of corn. As to suitable poultry rations this bulletin says:
Experiment has shown that the early stage of the chick's life, or that during which what are known as "starter feeds" are fed, is the critical period in so far as nutrition is concerned. Consequently the compounding of rations for this period, ordinarily the first eight to ten weeks of the chick's life, requires great care.
As pointed out above, owing to ahe chick's comparatively tender digestion at this stage the caution as to keeping down fibre in the ration applies particularly at this time.
I ask hon. members to note this:
As a consequence it is suggested that barley should not be substituted for corn meal to any extent in the starter ration.

Was that written by an
agricultural student or by a practical man?

You must ask the Minister of Agriculture for that information, this is his bulletin. It is true that the poultrymen in British Columbia did use a little more barley some time ago, but there were reasons for that: first, the farmers in Manitoba were practically giving their barley away so that it was much cheaper than corn; second, the poultrymen were practically giving their eggs away and were looking around for some grain at a price that would enable them to produce
eggs much cheaper than had been possible before. I think they would have use anything had it been practicable.
The other day I was noticing our importations of com from the Argentine. Last year we exported to the Argentina over $19,000,000 of goods, and we imported from them over $10,000,000 worth of goods, but I ask the committee to note that nearly half of our importations represented corn. I am afraid our good-will mission won't sound so good to the people of the Argentine when they learn that this duty has been placed on practically half of our importations from their country.

No, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth is speaking to a point which I conceded, namely that corn might be useful to the poultry industry. [DOT]

With all due respect to the hon. member for Stanstead and the Prime Minister, I think the farmers of Nova Scotia had better be consulted as to what they are going to use for feed rather than to have a tax and penalty placed on them for using the feed they think is 'best adapted to their purpose.
