speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: What would the farmers of 'Nova Scotia say if they were told that there are other farmers in Canada who would like to sell something to replace corn?

It is not corn we are talking about in particular. The government are trying to tell the fanners of Nova Scotia that they must use barley rather than com, because the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Stanstead know better what they should use than they know themselves.

On behalf of the poultry farmers of the Fraser valley I am only asking a fair chance to compete. We now compete in the world markets with our eggs; there are more eggs being produced in Canada than can be consumed here. We are looking for markets abroad, and on behalf of the poultry-men I am only asking that they be given a fair opportunity. Even if corn were grown in Canada the Pacific slope is too far removed from the corn area for that to be of much help. We are even far removed from the barley of Manitoba, and with the high freight rates barley costs between 826 and $30 a ton. This year we are able to buy greater quantities of barley because the farmers of Manitoba have been practically giving away that grain.

Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? What would the poultry farmers of British Columbia think if 
the protection on their product were removed? This measure only extends to the farmers of the prairies the protection already given the poultrymen of the Fraser valley.

I do not think the poultry-men would be very agreeable to that, but I assure my hon. friend that the protection given the poultrymen did not in any way hurt the purchaser of eggs on the prairies, because eggs have been cheaper there than ever before. The purchaser of eggs has been able to buy them for much less than ever before, even with the protection. The situation in the Fraser valley is almost pathetic this year. We have great areas of costly land there adapted only to this use, and I believe that since the first of January almost
100,000	birds have been slaughtered by men trying to meet their bills and others who have beer, forced to liquidate. This duty will be an additional burden, because com cannot be entirely dispensed with. The four grains are required, and corn is a far more suitable ration than barley which, as I said before, contains too much fibre. I could go on at greater length and give further statistics, but I do not think it is necessary. If we in British Columbia are to be denied corn I think the Prime Minister should consider very carefully a reduction in freight rates when that question comes before the house. If we are to be compelled to use Canadian grains only surely we on the Pacific slope should be able to purchase those grains as cheaply as they can be purchased in Japan or China. I must protest as strongly as possible against the imposition of this 25 cent duty.

I should like to associate myself with the protests expressed by the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth and the hon. member for New Westminster. I realize that if the Prime Minister has set his heart on the imposition of a 25 cent duty on com that duty will be imposed; I hardly expect my protest to have any effect, but in justice to my constituents who have written me in large numbers protesting against this duty on com, I must say what I am now stating to the committee. I think there is nothing that has caused a greater outcry in my constituency than this proposed duty. The people who are raising poultry and producing beef and pork are up in arms against the government on this matter, and I wish to convey that message to the Prime Minister and ask him to reconsider his action.

Replying to the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster, I want to speak particularly in regard to the

efficacy of feeding barley rather than corn. The hon. member says that in the first place it is more expensive. I dealt with this matter earlier in the session, and I think I proved to the satisfaction of the house that barley is cheaper on the Pacific coast than corn. If you take the hull off the barley would it be as cheap? Corn is a whole grain.

You can feed it as it is. In the first place I want to put this point before the committee, that barley is cheaper than corn, and in the second place I want to submit that barley is equally as good as corn for the feeding of poultry. I want to tell you why I make that statement. I refer to a series of pamphlets issued by the Department of Agriculture; if my hon. friend will turn to No. 128 of the new series he will find the material which on a previous occasion I placed before the house. In the second place I would refer him to experiments which have just been concluded at the Manitoba agricultural college, which have proved that for feeding purposes barley is better than corn. Those experiments were carried on over a period of two years.
Other hon. members have said that they cannot feed barley, that they must feed corn. That is a matter for experimentation; they do not feed barley because they have not done so previously. It is not because they cannot do so or because it is not equally good. Remember that the world's champion hen came from Saskatchewan, and it never had a bit of corn.
It came from British Columbia, not Saskatchewan.

That is quite correct, but
some three years ago the world's champion hen came from Saskatchewan, and it was not fed corn at all. So far as statistics are concerned, expert testimony can be given on both sides. But what the hon. member forgets is that on the coast he is getting protection for his fruit and his lumber and for everything which he produces and we are buying these things on the prairies. But when the tables are turned and we have something to sell which is cheaper than corn then he objects.

What protection is there on
lumber?

You get protection on
various articles, particularly on fruit and
vegetables; and there is also the question of freight rates. I say however that no one can prove, under any circumstances, that barley cannot successfully be fed as' well as corn. Remember that there are in the west 100,000,000 bushels of barley which cannot be sold except to the Canadian people. Let the hon. member bear in mind that there are other provinces besides British Columbia which he must help, just as the rest of Canada helps his province. This is one of the best measures we have had proposed in this country looking to the creation of a market for barley.

I do not wish to enter
into the controversy about the origin of the old hen. Whether she came from Saskatchewan or from British Columbia is a matter which history will undoubtedly record. The farmers in the eastern townships have always used corn and no doubt this duty will upset a very well established usage and trade in that area. I believe however that the farming community of the eastern townships, in the spirit in which they receive protection for their commodities, will be willing that the grain growers on the prairies receive like benefits for their products. I think I know my own people well. I believe that, despite any inconvenience they may experience, they will be willing at least to make the attempt to use Canadian barley as a substitute for American and Argentine corn. I wish in passing, however, to say that they are somewhat concerned lest the grain merchants who have imported corn duty free attempt to avail themselves of the duty with respect to corn upon which no duty was paid. I ask that the departments charged with inspection in these matters keep an eye on any who might attempt to make an unfair profit.
Coming back to poultry, I can assure my hon. friend from New Westminster that not all poultry are chickens-

Nor all chickens
poultry.

Nor all chickens poultry. There are several very respectable members of the poultry family which do not glory in the name chicken. There are some that can swim. speechtext: This is importation for all purposes. There are four cornmeal mills in one county.

I am assuming that they will use corn. The Prime Minister might as well decide to put an embargo on tea because we produce milk, and so compel everyone to drink milk instead of tea. That would be just as logical. You could produce analyses to show that milk is an excellent food product and a good beverage, and on the strength of this my right hon. friend might compel us all to drink milk instead of tea. There is, I say, just as much logic in that as in compelling those engaged in a certain industry to use something else than the commodity which they require for their purposes. By the duty which he is putting on corn he is going to try to compel the farmers to use barley. In Nova Scotia we did think that the poultry business might survive. We have a water freight rate from the Argentine and we have an opportunity of selling to that country goods which we cannot sell to the central provinces, such as fish and coal. There must be food products imported into Canada against which my right hon. friend could impose an embargo, insisting that everyone eat fish, in order that fish produced in the maritime provinces might be sold.
There is a duty on fish.
The hon. gentleman knows we do not import fish.
Yes, we do.

a Nova Scotian, to declare in this house that he would like to see the duty on fish and coal abrogated?	[DOT]

It means $140,000 from Nova Scotia.

I may say to the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth that we purchased
69,000	bags of potatoes from his section and paid forty-nine and a half cents freight per bag to have them come into our county. We can sell the maritimes all the corn they want if they will pay the freight to haul it there, and we can produce 10,500,000 bushels of corn, enough to supply the whole Dominion.
I am sorry to see an hon. member from western Ontario rise in his place, and protest against a duty of twenty-five cents on corn. I think he will live to regret doing so.

It is curious to note that this debate regarding corn and hens has been carried on almost exclusively by members of the legal profession, with the exception only of the last speaker, whose name is generally more associated with onions than with corn; and the hon. member for New Westminster who really knows what he is talking about.

Will the hon. member permit me to say that with regard to ducks -and I may tell the hon. gentleman I know nothing about chickens and made no pronouncement regarding them-I happen to know something of them and any information I gave, to the committee rests upon experience.
I do not quite catch the idea.
I did not think you did.
The hon. member says he knows nothing about chickens, but the ideas he gave to the committee were founded upon experience. Experience of what?
Experience of ducks.
I am not dealing with ducks at the present time.
The hon. member is not. I was.

He did refer to chickens, and I will quote him presently. I just want to join with the hon. member for New Westminster in protesting against the imposition of this duty. People from the east do not perhaps realize the extent of the industry in British Columbia. In the old days hens were things that were generally kept around a farm in order to dirty up the machinery. When the farmer saw somebody coming, he grabbed one and killed it for lunch. I am told. We

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
are sometimes told: If the egg market is low, why do you not keep a few cows? But it must be realized that these egg farms number up to 5,000 or 6,000 birds which are kept on five acres of land that, on account of their being suitable for chickens, are not adaptable for growing grain or potatoes. Such land, being high and dry, is good for chickens, but not suitable for any other form of agriculture, and indeed, it is quite impossible to go into dairying or mixed farming on such a limited area as five acres. If people in the east could get that into their minds, they would see how important this matter is. The hon. member for New Westminster said that egg producing had reached the basis of an industrial proposition. That is exactly the case and a difference of a cent a dozen in the cost of the eggs means the difference between loss and profit.
I spoke on this subject on the budget, and therefore I shall not detain the committee. I made the remark that there were three things you could not deceive: mother nature, a laying hen and a milking cow. I have seen people who have tried to do that and they made a dismal failure of it. I have in mind a man who got control of a farm. He was one of your patent expert book farmers; he did it all out of a book. He decided, according to the analysis of certain foods, he had to feed his stock only certain things. This worked beautifully on paper until the animals began to starve and die. If I recollect right, one of his book doctrines was that hogs should fatten on cabbages. It was all laid out according to the analysis that with cabbages and some other addition, the hogs ought to do beautifully. The trouble was that they did not do beautifully; they died, or at least starved. He had proceeded along certain lines laid down in a book, without having the practical knowledge of the farmer. You cannot deceive a milking cow. You may talk of expert knowledge and technique all you like, but the cow's milk will go down if you do not feed her the feeds adapted to a big flow of milk. The same with eggs. You cannot miss even a couple of hours in feeding a flock of chickens without it being recorded in a day or so in the egg basket. They are very sensitive, and fussy, if I may use the word.
It is ridiculous to suggest that you can substitute barley for corn. You can, of course, but at the expense of the eggs. Certainly you can substitute barley to a certain exent, but you always must have a certain quantity of corn, not only for the reasons given by the hon. member for New Westminster, but also

because in winter there is a heat-giving property to corn that is not possessed by barley. Experience has shown that hens must have a certain quantity of com.
We have heard again and again, almost to the extent of being tired of it, that the policy of the government is to give Canadians an opportunity of competing with their competitors on even terms. I presume that the proposition of Euclid holds good in this case, that the greater includes the less, and that the term Canadians would also extend to Canadian hens. What we are asking is that Canadian hens shall have an equal opportunity to compete with those hens that get their corn at a much lower price.
The hon. member for Souris claimed that barley was cheaper than corn. Probably it is; but it is the relative value that counts. Because a thing is absolutely cheaper, it does not follow that it is really cheaper to use it. There are plenty of things that are cheaper than corn, oats or potatoes, for instance, but you must take into consideration their relative value. Apart from the relative value, corn must be used no matter what the price is. My hon. friend from Souris spoke of a duty on fruit helping British Columbia fruit growers, and said that that ought to compensate us for the heavy duty on corn. I would suggest that some of the other members from British Columbia deal with that and say if it will appeal to the poultry raisers as a satisfactory argument.
We have also been told, and we have just passed a resolution to that effect, that if there is any rise in price in consequence of the duty, the duty will be taken off. Then better not put it on in the first place. This particular item is not to come into force for one month, but immediately notice of the duty was given the price of com went up about $9 a ton.
The hon. member for Stanstead said that the members from British Columbia representing the poultry raisers should be content because we would fix our minds on the increased duty on the product we raise, on eggs. There is some logic in that, I admit. It was superior to all this talk about trying to cheat the hen by trying to feed it barley when it wants corn, but the answer to my hon. friend is this. It was very much thrown up at me during the campaign that I was standing for the Dunning budget, which I adhered to then and still believe in, although it is not so popular now as it was a year ago. I said in the campaign that I was adhering to the Dunning budget, which imposed, under the countervailing duties, ten or twelve cents a dozen on American eggs. They pointed out that my opponent advocated the fixed in-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
creased tariff that would be imposed by the party that he represented if it came into office, and in the budget of last September we find that the Prime Minister gave expression to that principle. But there was this difference. He did not raise the duty on eggs any higher than it would have been under the countervailing duties. I think he himself said that that was true, speaking generally, with respect to the whole budget. He took the figure as it would have been arrived at under the Dunning budget and made that a fixed rate, and pointed out that there was an advantage in having it fixed and known, that people could count upon it, that that was better than under the countervailing duties of Mr. Dunning's budget, where the rates were liable to go down at times. But there was this great difference, and this is the answer to the hon. member for Stanstead, that the Dunning budget did not ask the poultrymen to pay through the nose for this privilege. Under the countervailing duties of the Dunning budget they were given a duty of ten or twelve cents a dozen, as the case might be, against American eggs, and it might go higher if necessary, but the Dunning budget did not say that those duties were to be accompanied by a huge increase in the duties on everything that the poultryman had to buy, on his boots, his clothes, his incubators, and above all, on the feed that he feeds his hens. That is the answer to the suggestion that we ought to be satisfied with this duty. Under the Dunning budget we got the same duty against American eggs, and we did not have to pay this enormous tax-because it is an enormous tax-on the products that we use. When you remember how largely these feeds bulk in the cost of raising poultry, you will appreciate what a big difference it makes.
It is also correct what someone has already suggested, that in buying barley we are heavily handicapped by the excessive domestic freight rates on grain from the prairies to British Columbia. If the government would take cognizance of the case that has been put up in this house again and again this year for reducing the domestic rates to the same level as the export rates, a thing like this would not hit us so hard. Still the fact remains that we must buy corn even if the duty was one-half as much again as it is now. The person who has to pay this new duty is the poultry-man, and he is already at his wits' end to know how he is to make a living.

How much of this
corn is expected to be displaced by the barley? Approximately ten million bushels of corn are imported. Will that be reduced to about five million bushels?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I stated to the committee that ten million bushels of corn were imported for all purposes, including distilling, starch making, and for other purposes. The returns in the department do not indicate the quantity imported for each specific purpose, so I cannot very accurately answer the question. But we know that the production in Canada last year of Indian corn was roughly six million bushels. The corn used for dairy purposes in the silos of course is grown in Canada, and will continue to be grown for dairy purposes.
I cannot answer with respect to the other. I need hardly say to the hon. gentleman, who knows far better than I of the emergent condition existing with respect to coarse grains in Canada, that owing to conditions that need not be referred to again their value is practically nil except the product is sold in Canada. It is believed that this will assist to that end without placing any undue burden on those engaged in the production of chickens, upon which an extra valuation for duty purposes of thirty cents a pound has been given to protect the industry from unfair competition. The corn mills, which was the one thing urged on behalf of Nova Scotia, where small mills still continue to grind corn, will continue to require their raw material free of duty. So will the breakfast food producers, and, as I said, the starch makers and distilleries. The distilleries pay 7| per cent. That may not sound very good in some counties of Nova Scotia, but it is a fact at any rate.

This duty is imposed to encourage the barley growers, but the question arises, how much of an additional market will it give them? If it will give them an additional market for only three or four million bushels, and even that is problematical, is it worth while disturbing the whole poultry business for that amount? I appreciate the purpose of this duty on corn. There is no question as to what it is meant for. The question is what effect will it have? How many poultry producers will stop feeding corn to feed barley? Mighty few. For the reason that they want corn, and are going to have corn even if it is 25 cents dearer. Again, if barley is not substituted for corn you are just upsetting the whole apple cart with respect to the poultry growers for an infinitesimal advantage to the barley growers. I do not think the proposed duty will affect the price of barley one iota. It will merely give an additional market of three or four million bushels-a very small item when we consider that Manitoba alone produced 100,-

000,000 bushels of barley last year. I think it would be well to look into the advantages as compared with the disadvantages of the poultry industry. There would be some advantage in getting a market for probably
5,000,000 additional bushels of barley at most *if it materialized.
Is the hon. member opposed to a tariff being placed on corn?
I am opposed if it does more harm than good.
Oh, oh.
If it does more good than harm I am supporting it.

From the Argentine?

Do we not get a large quantity from Manchuria?

I am afraid that statement shatters the hopes of some of the men on the prairies who have been thinking of 25 cents.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Twenty-five from the United States.

My appeal to
the Prime Minister would be that this is a very serious matter for the farmers of the province of Ontario. Over fifty years ago there was a battle royal on the part of those farmers to import feeding corn duty free. After years of fighting not only throughout the country but in this House of Commons that commodity was placed on the free list I think that took place in 1807 and from that day to the present irrespective of what government has been in power, they have always

seen fit to allow Indian corn to come into thi3 country free of duty. I may say in the locality from which I come, throughout my life time we have fed a mixture of corn and grains to fat cattle and dairy cows.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The corn fed to the
dairy cows would be ensilage, would it not?

No; we have grown that corn, forty acres at a time, for silo purposes. We do not think however that it pays us in our section of the country to grow corn for grain purposes. There are some farmers who grow a small quantity for the feeding of poultry, and if they were not allowed to purchase it they might grow enough for their hogs. I would say to the Prime Minister however that this is a very serious matter. Hon. members who are engaged in agriculture know that we are locking to the British market for disposition of our beef animals and dairy pi oduets, and in that market we have to compete with the Irish and British farmers and the farmers from Denmark. All those men get their corn duty free, and they have always looked upon that commodity as one of their main grain foods. One of my cousins who was engaged in the grain business and the business of supplying feed to the dairymen of Paisley and Glasgow almost always made a practice of cutting up hay and straw and mixing grain with them. The manner in which they mixed those grains was determined by very careful feeding experiments which had been conducted for years by the experimental tables of the Rothamsted Experimental Station in England. That station has always been considered one of the most reliable in the world. Not only has that been the result of experiments conducted at that station but it is also the result of experiments conducted for many years by the farmers of Ontario.
With respect to the importation of com I may say that owing to the very emergent conditions existing among the farmers of the province of Ontario importations were somewhat less during the last year. The following table will give an idea of the importations:
Year	Number of bushels
1928		 14,999,000
1929		 14,128,000

1931		 10,055,000
I may say that those figures are given for the fiscal years ending March 31.
Without exception in years gone by we have had imported into the constituency from which I come many carloads of corn for feeding

purposes, and it will be a distinct disadvantage to the farmers of that section of the province of Ontario-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow a question?-he is always most courteous in that regard. How many bushels of Indian corn did he purchase in the year for his farm and cattle? I should like to have an idea of an average purchase.

I may tell you, sir, that until ten years ago I conducted my farming operations as vigorously as possible. However at the end of that year my eldest son passed away. For years before that time we used to buy two carloads of corn or about
2,000	bushels per year. Previous to the time Indian corn was allowed in free we purchased corn from the counties of Essex and Kent. For two years those purchases were made but were never a success because the corn of those counties had so much moisture in it that in large quantities it would not keep. After purchasing that corn for two years we discontinued the practice.
The hon. member has spoken about moisture in Essex and Kent county corn. I should like to tell him there will be no moisture this year because in each county a drier has been installed.

I wish to plead further with the Prime Minister. As farmers we should like to have the privilege, concerning which he has spoken many times in this house, of equal opportunity and fair competition. If this privilege is withdrawn from the province of Ontario it is withdrawing one of the greatest privileges the farmers in that province have enjoyed for many years in the business of live stock feeding.
I would suggest that the hon. member speak for his own county.

I have been very much interested in this discussion in regard to the relative feeding values of barley and corn. We western farmers are interested in the duty because no doubt we have lots of barley to sell, and we are anxious to get our coarse grains on the market. But for the life of me I cannot see how this duty on corn is going to help us one iota. The member for South Essex tells us the farmers in his constituency are going to supply us with our corn and that this duty will boost the price.
I did not say that.

The economic condition of the farmers in western Canada and indeed throughout the country is so serious today that they want to get their barley cheaper. We want to get our barley down to eastern Canada cheaper. We want to lower freight rates so we can sell our barley and displace corn in the eastern markets. This duty will not enable us to do so. Many a farmer throughout the country believes firmlj- in his heart that nothing can take the place of corn when you come to fatten cattle. You cannot get the fat interwoven 'between the lean by feeding barley, you can only do it by feeding , corn. Many of our farmers know this, and the abattoir men also know it. That is why so many of them believe that corn is better than barley for feeding cattle. This duty will not do the farmers of eastern Canada one particle of good, nor will it help the farmers of western Canada to dispose of their barley. We want reduced freight rates so we can get our barley down here to displace corn.

I have listened with a good deal of attention to these professional men, and I wonder how many of them have used barley and corn for feeding purposes. The Prime Minister is absolutely correct in placing a duty on corn in the interests of the farmers of this country. In my constituency of Marquette barley is selling at eight and ten cents a bushel, and the farmers all over Manitoba have been appealing to us to get a duty placed on corn. As to the relative feeding values of corn and barley,
I have fed barley and I have fed corn, and I have made better gains feeding barley to my cattle than I ever did feeding them com. I prefer barley to corn any time, if it is handled by a proper feeder.
I wonder if some hon. gentlemen ever think of any other part of Canada but just their own little home circles-there are other parts of the dominion. Western Canada pressed for this duty to be placed on corn to help the western producer of coarse grains, that is, the man struggling on the land.
You were feeding big three or four year old steers were you?

I was feeding mature
cattle outside the city of Winnipeg and made a gain of two and a quarter pounds a day feeding barley; when I fed corn that I imported from the United States in carload lots I made a gain of only two pounds a day.
You were not giving them enough.

I can make better gains on barley than on corn; so can anybody if he handles the feed properly.

As a farmer of western
Canada I know something of the feed value of barley. I think hon. members from Saskatchewan will at least endorse what I am going to say in connection with the feed value of barley for poultry. We have heard a good deal about chickens-I am going to mention turkeys. I think the flavour of the turkeys that we raise in Saskatchewan is unsurpassed, and we feed them on barley.

Except those of the
county of Charlevoix.

I endorse what the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) has said. I have fed barley to feeder steers. I think hon. members from Saskatchewan will also endorse what I am going to say, unless they have had no experience, and it seems to me that some of them have not.
Do you mean to say I am not a farmer?
You cannot have had much experience feeding cattle or turkeys.
I farm three times the amount of land you do.
I am not a doctor, I am a farmer, and I am talking from practical experience as a farmer.
So am I.

I think the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) will have to acknowledge that we in the west more than hold our own in the feeding of cattle for export. It is surprising to me that hon. members on the opposite side take such an antagonistic attitude with respect to this duty on corn, especially after the speech which the hon. member for Willow Bunch made on the address, in the course of which he criticized the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks) for not taking the active part he should take in endorsing what he had said in favour of protecting the agriculturist all along the line. Now he is opposing the very thing I endorsed in my speech on the address. At that time 1 said I had a mandate from my constituents asking for protection. I do not know what the people of Saskatchewan will say to the hon. member for Willow Bunch and his friends when they go back home.
We will take a chance.

I am glad we have a sufficient number of members on this side of the house to ensure the passing of these tariff increases. I know that in the constituency of

Rosetown I will get a lot of credit for supporting the duty on com. Last year during the campaign the Prime Minister said that portection meant protection for all, and I think his statement is being verified by the putting of this duty on corn. I should like hon. members from Ontario and from British Columbia to give us a little cooperation on these lines. We in the prairie provinces did not howl our heads off when British Columbia asked for protection for her fruit. We were willing to help them in that direction even if it cost us a little more for the fruit we consume on the prairies. I can assure my hon. friends from British Columbia that when once they get educated to feeding barley to their stock they will not go back to feeding corn. AYe have had such success in Saskatchewan in feeding barley to steers, turkeys and chickens that we are well satisfied.
AVe should have a uniform policy on the tariff. In my speech on the address I said I was confident that what I was recommending would be given consideration in due time, and here we are now given an opportunity to support this duty on com. It will be a great pleasure to me to go back to my constituency and tell the farmers that, as the Prime Minister said during the campaign, protection means protection for all for farmers as well as for manufacturers. We have heard much from hon. members opposite against the various tariff items. As a farmer from Saskatchewan I should like to relpeat that the western farmers are not all opposed to increased duties, as one might imagine after listening to members opposite representing western constituencies. As I have said before this session, in my constituency, I think I was up against one of the greatest free traders in Canada, although my hon. friend from Weytburn (Mr. Young) might compete with the gentleman who opposed me, Mr. John Evans, who I understand is quite a free trader. At any rate I am glad to say that we are well satisfied to give this change a trial to see what the result will be. Most of us in the west are. still big enough to cooperate with the other parts of the dominion, and we only ask for fair play from the people of British Columbia. If we have, a chance I think we will be able to educate the people of that province, so they have nothing to fear from the tariff on corn. The hon. member for Souris has spoken of the tests which have been carried on, and I'hope the Saskatchewan members particularly will see their way clear to support this measure. We admit that things are bad in Saskatchewan; we would

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
like an outlet for our barley. We are going to have that outlet now, and we are glad to receive the support of the east. I am not criticizing the hon. members from British Columbia; their opposition is due to lack of education and nothing else, and we will overlook that.

I think too much has been said about British Columbia, particularly with regard to our lack of education; I cannot let that go by. No one could be more patriotic in buying Canadian products than the poul-trymen of British Columbia, but they believe in fair play. When they see people in foreign countries purchasing Canadian grain for less than we in British Columbia can purchase it, naturally they protest against any imposition of this kind. With reference to the feeding of turkeys I can tell my hon. friend that in British Columbia turkeys fed on wheat and corn command a price much greater than that paid for turkeys from Saskatchewan. If hon. members do not believe that statement I can get the figures.

I think
our farmer friends are unduly alarmed about this duty. The poultrymen will have to pay a little more for their corn, but the price of barley will not be increased. If it is any comfort to my Conservative friends in western Canada they can go home and tell their constituents they have put a duty on corn which they hope will increase the price of barley, but their constituents will have to be very gullible to believe that this will help them in any way. Hon. gentlemen opposite told the people of Canada that by putting a duty on butter the price would be increased, and that the same thing would happen in connection with beef, but we are exporting these commodities and will continue to do so, and the prices in foreign countries will continue to fix the prices at home. So I am not very much alarmed about the duty on corn. The poor old poultryman will have to pay the duty, that is all; the Ontario fanner who of necessity must use some corn will pay the duty also. As far as we are concerned in western Canada it is just so much eyewash with regard to getting an increased price for cur barley.

Could the Prime Minister
tell us about how many bushels of barley he hopes to be able to market by this measure?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I intimated to the committee that since there was no separation of items I could not give any accurate information in that regard. That question was asked
by the former Minister of Agriculture. Professor Grant of the Manitoba agricultural cdllege gave a great deal of study to this matter. It will be remembered that he was employed as an expert by the former advisory board, and I am indebted to one hon. member of the house for a copy of the report he made upon the use of barley instead of corn. He closes his report with these words:
The necessity for these imports in the light of our present knowledge may be seriously doubted. Evidently the traditionary practice or the aping of "corn belt" feeding outweighs other considerations. The Canadian wheat pool, backed by authorities and experiment station records is, at the present time, putting on an intensive educational campaign to sell the merits of Canadian barley to eastern feeders of live stock.
He deals with the question at some length. This is rather an interesting document to the layman who is neither a chicken fancier nor an agriculturist. All I can say is that I believe the result of this effort will be at least to ascertain with certainty the relative values of barley and corn for the purposes indicated. Other governments have had this matter in mind on previous occasions, when the emergency was not so great and conditions wer* not so bad. I believe this will stimulate the use of barley for the purposes indicated by the report.

Rather a costly experiment
I think.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think not.

I was pleased indeed to hear the remarks of my right hon. friend the Minister of Finance but when ha speaks of the results of experiments with regard to the feeding of barley in comparison with corn I am satisfied that those experiments have not been conducted for a sufficiently long period to give a justifiable result. I may tell hon. members of this house that I was brought up at the feet of men such as Doctor Mills, Professor C. A. Zavitz, Professor Panton and Professor George E. Day, and those men
They are all dead now.

No, they are
not, but those who have passed away, Professor Mills and Professor Panton, will be remembered as long as agriculture continues to exist in this country.
